To all 2025 & 2026 grads who’ve been DMing me for job guidance, I feel you, i have gone through all this as i could also not get anything on campus which is easier to crack comparatively.

I’ve gotten a ton of messages from juniors asking for help with the job search. I can’t reply to everyone individually, so I’m putting all my advice here.

If you’re hunting for your first role, do these 4 things every single day:

1. Search LinkedIn actively– Look for both internships and apprenticeships. At this stage, experience > job title. A 3-6 month apprenticeship can easily convert to full-time and beats having a gap. Use filters: “Past 24 hours”, “Internship”, “Entry level”,sort by most recent.

2. Update your Naukri.com daily– Add a skill, tweak one line in your summary, anything. Recruiters sort by “last updated”, so fresh profiles show up first. That tiny update matters.

3. Ask for referrals — don’t be shy– Find people from your target company on LinkedIn and send a short note:Hi [Name], I’m a 2025 or 26 grad seeking SDE intern roles at [Company]. If there are openings, could I share my resume for a referral? Thanks!Yes, 80% won’t even see it. But the 20% who do can change everything.

4.Apply more, overthink less – 100+ applications is normal. I was there too. You have to collect a lot of “Unfortunately, we won’t move forward” emails before you get the “Welcome to the team” one.
Remember: The first job is the hardest. Once you have _any_ experience — internship, apprenticeship, freelance, project — doors start opening. Something is always better than a resume gap.

I can’t get back to every DM, but I’m rooting for all of you. Show up daily. Your yes is coming.

It’s been a while! 👋 Let’s talk about something I’ve been diving back into: The Art of Bank Reconciliation.

I’ve been a bit quiet on LinkedIn lately as I’ve been focusing on upskilling and refining my workflow. But I’m back and excited to reconnect with this amazing community!
​To kick things off, I wanted to share a quick "back-to-basics" guide on something that remains the backbone of financial accuracy—Bank Reconciliation. Even with the best AI tools, the human touch is what ensures everything truly adds up.
​Here is my go-to process for a seamless reconciliation:
1. ​Match the Starting Line: Always ensure your internal book’s beginning balance matches the bank statement. If this is off, you’re chasing a ghost from the previous month.
2. ​The "In-Transit" Check: Identify deposits you've recorded that haven't hit the bank yet, and outstanding checks that haven't been cleared. These are the most common culprits for discrepancies.
3. ​Scan for Bank Artifacts: Look for those "hidden" items—service fees, interest earned, or even processing errors. They need to be adjusted in your books immediately.
4. ​The Final Verification: Once adjusted, your "Adjusted Bank Balance" must equal your "Adjusted Book Balance." If it doesn't, it’s time to look for transposed numbers (the classic "90" vs "09" error).

In my experience using systems like Accurate, QuickBooks Oonline and Odoo, automation helps, but understanding the logic behind the flow is what prevents year-end audit headaches.

I’m currently looking for new opportunities where I can bring this level of detail and my experience in financial operations to a forward-thinking team. If you’re hiring or know someone who is, let’s connect!

“Tere Instagram account ko kya hogaya?” 




A few weeks ago, I did something that felt… unnecessary at first.

I deleted Instagram.

Not because I hated it.
Not because I don’t love creating content.

In fact, I love content.
I love shooting reels 

But I realized something uncomfortable

I was consuming more than I was creating.
Scrolling more than I was thinking.
Watching more than I was doing.

So I tried an experiment.

I switched to LinkedIn.
Not just casually.

Full time. Till 1 am. Every day.

And I didn’t treat it like a “professional platform.”
I treated it like my only source of social media.

And everything HAS CHANGED. 

Instead of watching random reels,
Instead of liking posts,
I was starting conversations.

Instead of following influencers,
I was reaching out to Presidents, Directors, CEOs.

And the craziest thing?

Some of them replied.

That’s when it hit me

This platform is different.

On Instagram, attention is currency.
On LinkedIn, intent is currency.

Don’t get me wrong.

I’ll probably go back to Instagram soon.
I miss posting reels. I miss the chaos.

But this break showed me something important:

You don’t need more time.
You need better environments.

If you’ve been feeling stuck, distracted, or just… offfff

Maybe it’s not you.

Maybe it’s just the platform.

Eins will ich loswerden: LinkedIn ist wirklich krass.

Jeder nutzt diese Plattform auf seine eigene Art und Weise. Manche lesen still mit, manche kommentieren nur Unsinn aber: Richtig starke Persönlichkeiten sind oft nur eine Nachricht entfernt.

Man kann hier extrem viel lernen und sich richtig gut vernetzen. Viele sind überraschend offen und hilfsbereit. Besonders die, die unnahbar scheinen. 

LinkedIn bringt dich näher an Menschen, die ähnlich denken wie du. Aber auch an solche, die komplett anders ticken, weiter sind oder einfach mehr erlebt haben. 

An Menschen, die wirklich Lust haben, ihr Leben oder ihr Business besser zu machen. 

Feier ich. 

Und falls du dich schon mal gefragt hast, was ich eigentlich genau mache (für viele ist das scheinbar noch ein Fragezeichen): Vernetz dich mit mir, lass uns einfach sprechen. Lets go!

🎓 To everyone studying for their Workday certification at night after a full day of work. 

 I see you. 

 You open your notes after dinner when everyone else is watching TV. 

 You read about Business Processes and Security Groups when you would rather be doing anything else.

Everyone talks about ideas.

But here’s what most people don’t realize on LinkedIn:

👉 Ideas don’t get engagement. Structure does.

You can have the most brilliant thought in your head…
But if it’s not structured right, it gets ignored.

I’ve seen this happen too many times:

• Great insights → 10 likes
• Simple, well-structured posts → 10,000+ impressions

_________________________________________

So what’s really going on?

The truth about LinkedIn content

People don’t read posts.
They scan.

And structure is what makes them stop scrolling.

Here’s what actually works:

1. The Hook decides everything
If your first 2 lines don’t create curiosity, the rest of your post doesn’t matter.

Bad hook = dead post.

2. White space = readability
Big paragraphs kill attention.

Short lines → easier to read → more engagement.

3. Flow keeps them hooked
A good post feels like a conversation, not an essay.

• One idea per line
• Smooth transitions
• No unnecessary complexity

4. Formatting builds authority
Clean structure signals clarity of thought.

And clarity builds trust faster than “big ideas”.

_________________________________________

Here’s the shift most people need:

Stop asking:
❌ “Is my idea good enough?”

Start asking:
✅ “Is my idea easy to consume?”

Because on this platform:

The best writer doesn’t win.
The clearest one does.

_________________________________________

If you start focusing on structure, you’ll notice:

• Higher retention
• More saves
• Better conversations in DMs

And that’s where real opportunities begin.😉

It is about whether it feels intentional.

It is in the thinking behind it.

Using AI is not the issue.
The real question is what happens when it starts replacing taste, thinking, and originality in creative work.

Someone recently asked me how I continue to get top tier guests on my podcast.

And I had to think about it for a second.

5 years ago when I started it was folk from my network that I had been patiently building for half a decade.

After that I started shooting my shot. Reaching out on LinkedIn, X and via people I knew to reach others.

Some were referred by former guests as potentially interesting conversations.

But the one constant was persistentence.

When I interviewed Elizabeth Yin from Hustle Fund, it was over a year from first message to final conversation.

And there were many more like this.

Today?

I still do the same. I find interesting people that I would love to speak to and ask the question.

However, over the last 6 months or more I've seen an interesting shift...

I'm now getting a fair amount of inbound requests for some really stellar people to join me for a conversation.

But the lesson, if there is one, is this...

Whether it's a business, a newsletter or a podcast it starts with one.

And then the next.

And the next.

It's about showing up every time and treating every single client, guest or reader as if they were your first.

It's about being willing to be turned down - and lord knows that happens all the time.

But not letting one no put you off.

It's about playing the long game and not being a slave to the numbers.

About persistence, care and being proud of what you're putting out into the world.

And in the last five years that's gotten me to seven figures in my business and ~65k subscribers on the pod.

But I treat every day as if I'm just getting started.

Because too many people quit when they don't see immediate results, they assume all the stories they see on here or in the headlines happened overnight.

They don't see the time, the effort, the losses, the missteps along the way.

Nothing in life worth doing is easy.

You've got to put in the work.

Why your Nairobi business has 2,000 followers and zero enquiries. (It's not what you think.)

The LinkedIn algorithm is not your enemy. Your content strategy is.

I've audited 12+ Kenyan business profiles in the last 30 days. The same three mistakes appear every time:

1. The "About to Launch" trap — posting announcements instead of insights. Nobody cares you're launching. They care what problem you solve.

2. The Testimonial Graveyard — burying social proof 9 scrolls deep. If your best result isn't in your headline or your last 3 posts, it doesn't exist.

3. The Broadcast Voice — talking AT your audience instead of TO a specific person. LinkedIn rewards specificity. "Business owners in Nairobi who are tired of spending on ads with nothing to show" is a hook. "Business tips" is not.

Fix one of these this coming week. 

Start with number 2 — it takes 10 minutes and it will change your conversion rate.

« Every move matters. The partnership returns. SUITS 2 (2026) »

Ça vous parle ? À moi aussi… jusqu’à ce que je creuse un peu.

J’adore Suits. Vraiment. Cette série a su transformer le monde du droit corporatif en un véritable thriller psychologique : ego, loyauté, mensonges, rédemption… et ces dialogues assassins qui font mouche à chaque fois. 

Harvey Specter et Mike Ross restent, pour moi, l’un des duos les plus iconiques de la télévision.

Pourtant, cette affiche qui circule depuis plusieurs semaines est 100 % fake.

Aucune saison 10, aucun « Suits 2 » officiel n’a été annoncé par NBCUniversal, Aaron Korsh ou les acteurs principaux. 

Le spin-off Suits: L.A. (avec Stephen Amell) a été arrêté après une seule saison en 2025, et le retour du casting original (Gabriel Macht, Patrick J. Adams, Gina Torres, Sarah Rafferty) reste pour l’instant au stade de discussions hypothétiques, un film de réunion est parfois évoqué par le créateur et certains acteurs, mais rien de concret n’est en préparation pour 2026.

Cette illustration est un excellent exemple de #fakenews dans le divertissement : un montage soigné, un slogan percutant, une nostalgie parfaitement dosée… et des milliers de partages enthousiastes avant même qu’on vérifie les sources.

Pourquoi ça marche si bien ?

La série a connu un deuxième souffle massif sur Netflix, touchant une nouvelle génération.

Nous adorons les retrouvailles (« reunion ») : Friends, The Office, ou encore les rumeurs autour d’autres classiques.


Les algorithmes récompensent le contenu émotionnel et viral, même quand il est inventé.

Leçon professionnelle que j’en tire :

Dans notre monde ultra-connecté, la vitesse de propagation d’une information dépasse souvent sa véracité. Que ce soit pour une série culte, une opportunité business, une actualité corporate ou une rumeur sur un concurrent, un bon réflexe reste indispensable :

- Vérifier les sources officielles (Variety, Deadline, comptes des studios ou des acteurs).
- Prendre du recul face à l’émotion.
- Distinguer le désir (ce qu’on aimerait voir) de la réalité (ce qui est réellement annoncé)

Suits nous l’a si bien enseigné : la vérité finit toujours par sortir. Et quand elle sort, mieux vaut être du bon côté du tribunal… ou du feed LinkedIn.

Et vous, quelle est la série qui vous fait encore vibrer des années après ?

Avez-vous déjà été piégé par une fausse annonce de retour ou de suite ?

Dialysis is expensive. Kidney disease screening is not.

Cardiac surgery is expensive. Hypertension management is not.

Maternal emergency intervention is expensive. Skilled antenatal care is not.

Every health system that has ever underfunded prevention has eventually paid for it , at a cost that dwarfs the investment it refused to make. 💔

This is not a funding problem. It is an incentive problem dressed up as a funding problem.

Health systems are built to respond. Every budget cycle, every performance metric, every procurement conversation rewards the dramatic intervention , the surgery, the ICU bed, the emergency transfer. The nurse who caught the deterioration 48 hours earlier, the community health worker who identified the risk factor six months ago , their contribution is structurally invisible.

So it gets defunded. Quietly. In language that sounds responsible.
"We're rationalising our community health investment." "We're focusing resources on acute care capacity." "Prevention programs will resume when the budget allows."

The budget never allows. The downstream cost always arrives. 🔴

Many people asked me on DMs of my approach of getting Job Offers. 

Firstly, I didn’t restrict myself to any brand and get some clarity on the role by speaking to the professionals questions like how’s their day to day looks like, what are the business / service they deal with, what their seniors worked upon. And most importantly apply a salary filter whether we agree or not first thing we solve for is money. 

Then I create a target list of the companies offering the desired opportunities and then on linkedin I reach out to the people working over there. It’s important while reaching out, you need to target people with different designations differently. 

A VP referral holds much more weightage than an analyst whereas an analyst would give you much more clear picture regarding work flow. 

Follow a systematic approach, best is to create an excel tracker of let’s say you have reach out to someone on X day then follow up with them on X+4 day. Someone on Friday have told you that they will let you know on Monday then on Monday afternoon reach out to them. 

Never reach out to person on Monday morning, there is too much working piling up from weekends so your message most likely would get ignored.

Looking back at some of my old dashboards on LinkedIn, I can’t help but smile… 😅
I’ve come a long way—and that growth shows.

Here’s a hot take:
👉 Most dashboards look good… but don’t actually communicate anything.

Early on, I focused on making dashboards colourful—visually engaging and eye-catching.But real analytics isn’t about how colourful a dashboard looks.

It’s about how clearly it communicates.

It’s about making them impossible to misunderstand.

Because once your analysis is done and everything sits neatly on a dashboard…
what does your stakeholder actually see at first glance?

No explanation. No walkthrough. Just your work.

That’s the real test.

A strong dashboard is not just visual—it’s intentional.

🧠 Colour isn’t decoration, it’s communication
🔴 Red = risk, loss, urgency
🟢 Green = growth, stability, performance

📊 Every chart must answer a question
📖 Every layout must tell a story
🎯 Every element must drive a decision

And honestly… getting it right may sometimes make your dashboard look boring 😅
But that’s exactly the point.

If it’s clear, direct, and actionable—it’s doing its job.

Clarity over decoration.
Communication over aesthetics.

A dashboard shouldn’t always need you in the room to explain it.
It should speak, guide, and influence—on its own.

That’s what separates a dashboard… from a decision-making tool.

A career gap often signals resilience, responsibility, and grit — the exact traits companies claim to value until they show up in real life.

These candidates aren’t asking for sympathy.

Because the person who faced a crisis and came back stronger?

That’s not a hiring risk.

To all 2025 & 2026 grads who’ve been DMing me for job guidance, I feel you, i have gone through all this as i could also not get anything on campus which is easier to crack comparatively.

I’ve gotten a ton of messages from juniors asking for help with the job search. I can’t reply to everyone individually, so I’m putting all my advice here.

If you’re hunting for your first role, do these 4 things every single day:

1. Search LinkedIn actively– Look for both internships and apprenticeships. At this stage, experience > job title. A 3-6 month apprenticeship can easily convert to full-time and beats having a gap. Use filters: “Past 24 hours”, “Internship”, “Entry level”,sort by most recent.

2. Update your Naukri.com daily– Add a skill, tweak one line in your summary, anything. Recruiters sort by “last updated”, so fresh profiles show up first. That tiny update matters.

3. Ask for referrals — don’t be shy– Find people from your target company on LinkedIn and send a short note:Hi [Name], I’m a 2025 or 26 grad seeking SDE intern roles at [Company]. If there are openings, could I share my resume for a referral? Thanks!Yes, 80% won’t even see it. But the 20% who do can change everything.

4.Apply more, overthink less – 100+ applications is normal. I was there too. You have to collect a lot of “Unfortunately, we won’t move forward” emails before you get the “Welcome to the team” one.
Remember: The first job is the hardest. Once you have _any_ experience — internship, apprenticeship, freelance, project — doors start opening. Something is always better than a resume gap.

I can’t get back to every DM, but I’m rooting for all of you. Show up daily. Your yes is coming.

It’s been a while! 👋 Let’s talk about something I’ve been diving back into: The Art of Bank Reconciliation.

I’ve been a bit quiet on LinkedIn lately as I’ve been focusing on upskilling and refining my workflow. But I’m back and excited to reconnect with this amazing community!
​To kick things off, I wanted to share a quick "back-to-basics" guide on something that remains the backbone of financial accuracy—Bank Reconciliation. Even with the best AI tools, the human touch is what ensures everything truly adds up.
​Here is my go-to process for a seamless reconciliation:
1. ​Match the Starting Line: Always ensure your internal book’s beginning balance matches the bank statement. If this is off, you’re chasing a ghost from the previous month.
2. ​The "In-Transit" Check: Identify deposits you've recorded that haven't hit the bank yet, and outstanding checks that haven't been cleared. These are the most common culprits for discrepancies.
3. ​Scan for Bank Artifacts: Look for those "hidden" items—service fees, interest earned, or even processing errors. They need to be adjusted in your books immediately.
4. ​The Final Verification: Once adjusted, your "Adjusted Bank Balance" must equal your "Adjusted Book Balance." If it doesn't, it’s time to look for transposed numbers (the classic "90" vs "09" error).

In my experience using systems like Accurate, QuickBooks Oonline and Odoo, automation helps, but understanding the logic behind the flow is what prevents year-end audit headaches.

I’m currently looking for new opportunities where I can bring this level of detail and my experience in financial operations to a forward-thinking team. If you’re hiring or know someone who is, let’s connect!

A few weeks ago, I did something that felt… unnecessary at first.

I deleted Instagram.

Not because I hated it.
Not because I don’t love creating content.

In fact, I love content.
I love shooting reels 

But I realized something uncomfortable

I was consuming more than I was creating.
Scrolling more than I was thinking.
Watching more than I was doing.

So I tried an experiment.

I switched to LinkedIn.
Not just casually.

Full time. Till 1 am. Every day.

And I didn’t treat it like a “professional platform.”
I treated it like my only source of social media.

And everything HAS CHANGED. 

Instead of watching random reels,
Instead of liking posts,
I was starting conversations.

Instead of following influencers,
I was reaching out to Presidents, Directors, CEOs.

And the craziest thing?

Some of them replied.

That’s when it hit me

This platform is different.

On Instagram, attention is currency.
On LinkedIn, intent is currency.

Don’t get me wrong.

I’ll probably go back to Instagram soon.
I miss posting reels. I miss the chaos.

But this break showed me something important:

You don’t need more time.
You need better environments.

If you’ve been feeling stuck, distracted, or just… offfff

Maybe it’s not you.

Maybe it’s just the platform.

Eins will ich loswerden: LinkedIn ist wirklich krass.

Jeder nutzt diese Plattform auf seine eigene Art und Weise. Manche lesen still mit, manche kommentieren nur Unsinn aber: Richtig starke Persönlichkeiten sind oft nur eine Nachricht entfernt.

Man kann hier extrem viel lernen und sich richtig gut vernetzen. Viele sind überraschend offen und hilfsbereit. Besonders die, die unnahbar scheinen. 

LinkedIn bringt dich näher an Menschen, die ähnlich denken wie du. Aber auch an solche, die komplett anders ticken, weiter sind oder einfach mehr erlebt haben. 

An Menschen, die wirklich Lust haben, ihr Leben oder ihr Business besser zu machen. 

Feier ich. 

Und falls du dich schon mal gefragt hast, was ich eigentlich genau mache (für viele ist das scheinbar noch ein Fragezeichen): Vernetz dich mit mir, lass uns einfach sprechen. Lets go!

Everyone talks about ideas.

But here’s what most people don’t realize on LinkedIn:

👉 Ideas don’t get engagement. Structure does.

You can have the most brilliant thought in your head…
But if it’s not structured right, it gets ignored.

I’ve seen this happen too many times:

• Great insights → 10 likes
• Simple, well-structured posts → 10,000+ impressions

_________________________________________

So what’s really going on?

The truth about LinkedIn content

People don’t read posts.
They scan.

And structure is what makes them stop scrolling.

Here’s what actually works:

1. The Hook decides everything
If your first 2 lines don’t create curiosity, the rest of your post doesn’t matter.

Bad hook = dead post.

2. White space = readability
Big paragraphs kill attention.

Short lines → easier to read → more engagement.

3. Flow keeps them hooked
A good post feels like a conversation, not an essay.

• One idea per line
• Smooth transitions
• No unnecessary complexity

4. Formatting builds authority
Clean structure signals clarity of thought.

And clarity builds trust faster than “big ideas”.

_________________________________________

Here’s the shift most people need:

Stop asking:
❌ “Is my idea good enough?”

Start asking:
✅ “Is my idea easy to consume?”

Because on this platform:

The best writer doesn’t win.
The clearest one does.

_________________________________________

If you start focusing on structure, you’ll notice:

• Higher retention
• More saves
• Better conversations in DMs

And that’s where real opportunities begin.😉

Someone recently asked me how I continue to get top tier guests on my podcast.

And I had to think about it for a second.

5 years ago when I started it was folk from my network that I had been patiently building for half a decade.

After that I started shooting my shot. Reaching out on LinkedIn, X and via people I knew to reach others.

Some were referred by former guests as potentially interesting conversations.

But the one constant was persistentence.

When I interviewed Elizabeth Yin from Hustle Fund, it was over a year from first message to final conversation.

And there were many more like this.

Today?

I still do the same. I find interesting people that I would love to speak to and ask the question.

However, over the last 6 months or more I've seen an interesting shift...

I'm now getting a fair amount of inbound requests for some really stellar people to join me for a conversation.

But the lesson, if there is one, is this...

Whether it's a business, a newsletter or a podcast it starts with one.

And then the next.

And the next.

It's about showing up every time and treating every single client, guest or reader as if they were your first.

It's about being willing to be turned down - and lord knows that happens all the time.

But not letting one no put you off.

It's about playing the long game and not being a slave to the numbers.

About persistence, care and being proud of what you're putting out into the world.

And in the last five years that's gotten me to seven figures in my business and ~65k subscribers on the pod.

But I treat every day as if I'm just getting started.

Because too many people quit when they don't see immediate results, they assume all the stories they see on here or in the headlines happened overnight.

They don't see the time, the effort, the losses, the missteps along the way.

Nothing in life worth doing is easy.

You've got to put in the work.

« Every move matters. The partnership returns. SUITS 2 (2026) »

Ça vous parle ? À moi aussi… jusqu’à ce que je creuse un peu.

J’adore Suits. Vraiment. Cette série a su transformer le monde du droit corporatif en un véritable thriller psychologique : ego, loyauté, mensonges, rédemption… et ces dialogues assassins qui font mouche à chaque fois. 

Harvey Specter et Mike Ross restent, pour moi, l’un des duos les plus iconiques de la télévision.

Pourtant, cette affiche qui circule depuis plusieurs semaines est 100 % fake.

Aucune saison 10, aucun « Suits 2 » officiel n’a été annoncé par NBCUniversal, Aaron Korsh ou les acteurs principaux. 

Le spin-off Suits: L.A. (avec Stephen Amell) a été arrêté après une seule saison en 2025, et le retour du casting original (Gabriel Macht, Patrick J. Adams, Gina Torres, Sarah Rafferty) reste pour l’instant au stade de discussions hypothétiques, un film de réunion est parfois évoqué par le créateur et certains acteurs, mais rien de concret n’est en préparation pour 2026.

Cette illustration est un excellent exemple de #fakenews dans le divertissement : un montage soigné, un slogan percutant, une nostalgie parfaitement dosée… et des milliers de partages enthousiastes avant même qu’on vérifie les sources.

Pourquoi ça marche si bien ?

La série a connu un deuxième souffle massif sur Netflix, touchant une nouvelle génération.

Nous adorons les retrouvailles (« reunion ») : Friends, The Office, ou encore les rumeurs autour d’autres classiques.


Les algorithmes récompensent le contenu émotionnel et viral, même quand il est inventé.

Leçon professionnelle que j’en tire :

Dans notre monde ultra-connecté, la vitesse de propagation d’une information dépasse souvent sa véracité. Que ce soit pour une série culte, une opportunité business, une actualité corporate ou une rumeur sur un concurrent, un bon réflexe reste indispensable :

- Vérifier les sources officielles (Variety, Deadline, comptes des studios ou des acteurs).
- Prendre du recul face à l’émotion.
- Distinguer le désir (ce qu’on aimerait voir) de la réalité (ce qui est réellement annoncé)

Suits nous l’a si bien enseigné : la vérité finit toujours par sortir. Et quand elle sort, mieux vaut être du bon côté du tribunal… ou du feed LinkedIn.

Et vous, quelle est la série qui vous fait encore vibrer des années après ?

Avez-vous déjà été piégé par une fausse annonce de retour ou de suite ?

We Keep Paying for the Cure. We Keep Cutting the Prevention.

Dialysis is expensive. Kidney disease screening is not.

Cardiac surgery is expensive. Hypertension management is not.

Maternal emergency intervention is expensive. Skilled antenatal care is not.

Every health system that has ever underfunded prevention has eventually paid for it , at a cost that dwarfs the investment it refused to make. 💔

This is not a funding problem. It is an incentive problem dressed up as a funding problem.

Health systems are built to respond. Every budget cycle, every performance metric, every procurement conversation rewards the dramatic intervention , the surgery, the ICU bed, the emergency transfer. The nurse who caught the deterioration 48 hours earlier, the community health worker who identified the risk factor six months ago , their contribution is structurally invisible.

So it gets defunded. Quietly. In language that sounds responsible.
"We're rationalising our community health investment." "We're focusing resources on acute care capacity." "Prevention programs will resume when the budget allows."

The budget never allows. The downstream cost always arrives. 🔴

Many people asked me on DMs of my approach of getting Job Offers.

Then I create a target list of the companies offering the desired opportunities and then on linkedin I reach out to the people working over there. It’s important while reaching out, you need to target people with different designations differently. 

A VP referral holds much more weightage than an analyst whereas an analyst would give you much more clear picture regarding work flow. 

Follow a systematic approach, best is to create an excel tracker of let’s say you have reach out to someone on X day then follow up with them on X+4 day. Someone on Friday have told you that they will let you know on Monday then on Monday afternoon reach out to them. 

Never reach out to person on Monday morning, there is too much working piling up from weekends so your message most likely would get ignored.

🌏 Insurance AI: 900+ use cases — and still not scaling 🔍 More use cases do not mean more scale Allianz reports more than 900 AI use cases internally registered worldwide. Yet, speaking at InsurTech Insights, Jason Howes of Allianz UK noted that scaling AI remains difficult, as reported by Insurance Post (Mar 19, 2026). This is not a contradiction. “900 use cases” does not mean 900 scaled deployments. It reflects a portfolio of initiatives — from pilots to partial implementations — across the group. AI is already widespread. But most use cases remain local. They work within specific teams, on specific workflows, under specific assumptions. What they rarely do is scale across: systems workflows decision ownership That is where scaling becomes difficult. ⸻ ⚖️ Not a regulatory issue The EU, under the EU AI Act, pushes for structured, risk-based deployment. The UK, guided by institutions such as the Financial Conduct Authority, takes a more principles-based approach. Different models. Same pattern. Even in more flexible environments, AI does not automatically scale. Because the constraint is not regulatory permission. It is operational integration. ⸻ 🧩 What this means for insurers Scaling AI is not about launching more use cases. It requires: • standardising workflows where decisions can be made • defining clear ownership of AI-driven decisions • designing systems to integrate, not isolate, AI capabilities Without this, AI remains a collection of initiatives rather than an operating capability. ⸻ 🧭 Key message AI does not fail at scale because of individual firms. It fails because large organisations are not designed to absorb it consistently. 猿渡哲也氏は『高校鉄拳伝タフ』、『TOUGH-タフ-』などシリーズ作をヒットさせ、現在は『TOUGH 龍を継ぐ男』を連載中。シリーズ累計発行部数は1000万部を突破している。 『高校鉄拳伝タフ』や『TOUGH-タフ-』の主人公である宮沢熹一（キー坊）は、当初はお調子者だが、格闘家としてさまざまな死線をくぐり抜ける中で次第に成長を遂げていく。 迫力ある作画で描かれる格闘シーンは読者に強いインパクトをもたらし、また台詞もあわせたそのキャッチーさはたびたび読者のあいだで話題になる。キー坊の「ウ…ウソやろ こ…こんなことが こんなことが許されていいのか」の1コマを知っている人は多いことだろう。

『高校鉄拳伝タフ』

ほかにも、先日には所ジョージさんが司会を務める日テレのテレビ番組『1億人の大質問!?笑ってコラえて！』の街頭インタビューで偶然にも猿渡氏が登場したことでも話題に。なにかと『タフ』や猿渡氏自身への言及がネット上で増えていたタイミングでのアカウント開設となった形だ。 今後のコミックスの発刊やイベントの告知などの情報発信をX（Twitter）アカウントで行っていくとのことで、さっそく『ブラック・エンジェルズ』の作者・平松伸二氏と共同で行う握手会が開催される“ひめじSubかる☆フェスティバル”に関する投稿をリポスト（リツイート）している。

A small cultural note that makes a big difference

In working with colleagues in Japan, one small detail can go a long way: the use of “-san.” Using “-san” isn’t just a linguistic habit — it’s a simple expression of respect, professionalism, and equality. While it’s perfectly fine to call someone by their first name without “-san,” using a last name without any honorific (for example, calling someone just “Yamada”) can come across as disrespectful.

From my own experience, being addressed by last name only usually happened in very specific contexts — school, among close friends, or in highly hierarchical environments. Even then, I personally avoided addressing others that way.

If someone calls me “Sugita (my last name)” without an honorific, I usually ask them to use “Kats (my first name)” or “Sugita‑san,” regardless of our relationship. Not because of formality — but because respect matters, and it’s often conveyed through small, thoughtful actions.

Being mindful of these nuances helps build trust and makes cross‑cultural collaboration smoother for everyone.

Ekiden: A Lesson in Shared Purpose, Resilience—and Grace in Defeat

Every January, millions in Japan tune in to watch the Hakone Ekiden, a two-day, 217 km (135 mile) university relay race. It’s more than a sporting event—it’s a living example of leadership, teamwork, and character. The word Ekiden means “station to station,” rooted in an ancient courier system. Today, the sash (tasuki) symbolizes trust, responsibility, and continuity. Each runner pushes beyond personal limits, not for individual glory, but to honor the team and the shared goal. 

Sometimes, we witness something even more inspiring: grace in defeat.
I’ll never forget a team captain who gave a heartfelt speech after his team—expected to win after dominating two prior races—fell short. He thanked his general managers and teammates, made humble reflection of the race and then shouted, “I love my team!” despite the loss. Finally, he promised that his successors would win next year.
Moments like these remind us:
• We cannot always enjoy great business outcomes.
• Being a good loser—and learning from setbacks—is just as important as winning.
He embodied that spirit.

Ekiden is true teamwork:
• Success is a relay of effort, trust, and adaptability.
• Passing the baton—knowledge, responsibility, encouragement—is as critical as running your leg.
• Leadership means creating conditions where every runner feels their role is vital.

Every year, I cheer the runners in person. It’s my New Year ritual, and their determination gives me incredible energy. If you’re in Japan, I highly recommend experiencing it in person—or at least watching it on TV. You’ll gain a deeper understanding of Japanese culture and its emphasis on collective purpose: valuing the team over the individual, prioritizing endurance over speed, and cherishing the act of “passing on” responsibility. These principles are deeply woven into how Japanese organizations operate.

As we start a new year, let’s ask ourselves: “How can we design our teams to run like an Ekiden—aligned, resilient, and inspired by a common purpose?”

Great slides aren’t decoration—they’re strategy.

Too often we see the same deck used for a team update, an executive decision meeting, and a broad town hall. The result? Dense slides, tiny fonts, and audiences who can’t engage.

For me, slide design is both Inclusion and Business Effectiveness:
• Inclusion: Design for everyone in the room (and on the call). Use clear hierarchy, large readable fonts, high contrast, minimal jargon, and one message per slide. If people can’t read it, they can’t contribute.
• Plain Language for Global Audiences: Global leaders avoid overly sophisticated word choices because many listeners are non‑native English speakers. I appreciate that almost all Astellas senior leaders are mindful of this and consistently communicate so everyone can follow and contribute.
• Business Effectiveness: Tailor to the occasion. Executives need a crisp story and a clear “ask.” Broad communications need simplicity and clarity. Fewer, sharper slides improve decision velocity and alignment.

As leaders, our responsibility is to communicate accessibly and decide decisively. Let’s choose readability over density and clarity over completeness—and get better outcomes for our people and our business.

Inclusion at Astellas isn’t a slogan—it’s the way we turn innovative science into real‑world outcomes for patients. When we all stay relentlessly business‑oriented, inclusion becomes practical and measurable: we learn what the business needs, and we co‑create solutions that move the business.

• Topic
• Why now (why this deserves the meeting)
• Options (viable solutions)
• Today’s recommendation & why
• Timeline
• Cost proposal
Charts or a table can be attached, but only the one‑pager is presented on the day—because clarity invites diverse voices, focuses debate on decisions, and accelerates execution. At Astellas, if a proposal is not presented as a one‑pager, it will not be tabled for discussion or approval.

From my experience as CPO at Astellas, initiatives go well when we follow this guideline. When we don’t, even high‑quality proposals face challenges. The difference is business‑side buy‑in and understanding the audience—without those, HR initiatives risk becoming self‑satisfaction rather than business impact.
HR experts often default to technical explanations, but what the business truly needs is a clear line of sight to how the proposal drives our business—pipeline impact, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes. HR is part of the business, not adjacent to it. Thinking from that point of view is critical.
When we combine diverse perspectives with business rigor, we make faster, smarter decisions—and that’s how we win for patients and for Astellas.

As we step into 2026, I’d like to share a personal reflection—one that I’m still working through.
Delegation is something I continue to struggle with: handing things off sooner, clarifying outcomes, and truly letting the team lead. Recent 360-degree feedback shows some improvement, and I’m grateful for that. Still, I’m not satisfied with my progress, and I often feel frustrated with how slowly I’m changing.
As a non-native English speaker, I sometimes find my instructions aren’t as clear as I’d like, and I tend to micromanage. I recognize these are areas I need to improve, and I appreciate the patience of those who have experienced this.
The pressure to deliver results quickly in today’s world is real, and I feel it keenly. That pressure sometimes adds to my frustration, but it also reminds me how important it is to build trust and delegate more effectively.
My commitment for 2026 is to listen more, trust more, and create more space for growth—starting with my own. If anyone has faced similar challenges or found helpful approaches, I’d truly appreciate hearing your thoughts.

Active recovery - Japanese follows English
 
I hope you're all doing well. I wanted to share an interesting concept that's been beneficial for me: active recovery. It comes from the sports world, where it's understood that complete rest after intense activity (such as long distance races) isn't always the best approach. Instead, light exercise can actually help speed up and enhance recovery.
We all have busy lives, and it's common to hear people say they need to sleep all day on weekends. I sometimes feel that way too, but I've found that keeping my routine, even on weekends, is incredibly helpful. Having a dog really helps with this. Dogs don't understand the concept of days off, so they stick to their rhythm, which in turn helps me stick to mine. Even if I want to sleep in on Saturday, my dog wakes me up at 5 AM, just like any other day. 
Before having a dog, my weekend time management was more relaxed. But now, with this routine, I can get a lot done in the mornings on Saturdays and Sundays. I can go for a long-distance run, catch up on reading, and spend quality time with my wife discussing various topics. This sense of accomplishment and the extra energy it brings is quite rewarding.
Engaging in active recovery not only refreshes me but also promotes better balance. Exercise allows my brain to take a break and my muscles to release tension, leading to a more refreshed and balanced state. I hope you find this concept as beneficial as I do. Have a great day ahead!

What is a short-term assignment in Astellas? It really works well! 

I wanted to share some exciting news regarding the progress we've made with "short-term assignments" in Astellas. For those who might not be familiar, a short-term assignment is a 1-6 month stint in a different country. During this period, employees maintain their original responsibilities while also taking on some project-type initiatives at the new location.
 
The rationale behind these assignments is straightforward. Long-term assignments, such as those lasting 2-3 years, can sometimes be unfeasible for individuals due to family or other personal reasons. However, short-term assignments offer a more manageable alternative. While some may argue that a short duration isn't sufficient, I believe that any exposure is better than none. Of course, a longer period of 2-3 years or more would be ideal for in-depth learning, but short-term assignments can still provide valuable experiences and growth opportunities. Additionally, participating in a short-term assignment can pave the way for long-term assignments if needed later.
 
I've seen many individuals benefit immensely from these short-term assignments. Although there isn't an official program for short-term assignments, it's essentially an extended business trip, making it relatively easy to initiate. All it takes is a career conversation with our supervisor to identify the best opportunities for our development. Ideally, our expertise and experience will contribute to the success of the new location, creating a win-win situation for everyone involved.
 
I recently learned that some regions have 10-15 short-term assignees, which is fantastic! I believe we can achieve even more. I encourage our people to have career discussions with their supervisors and make their dreams a reality.

How to get control of our time

I recently came across a message that resonated with me, and I wanted to share it with all of you as I believe it could significantly enhance our workflow and communication. The message stated: "If I do not receive any response from you prior to [specified deadline], I will assume you have no edits to this latest draft, and I will proceed."
 
I think this approach is fantastic for maintaining a sense of urgency and ensuring that projects move forward without unnecessary delays. It is both polite and effective, and it fosters accountability. By not responding, you are essentially signaling trust and delegation, which can be very empowering.
 
Many years ago, I had the experience of working with a great supervisor who was in a different country. Despite their many strengths, their response speed was a weak point that often slowed down my work. This situation led to frustration and a realization that I needed a better way to manage communication. My mentor recommended the same proactive communication technique “if I don’t receive…”, and it dramatically changed my professional life.
 
By using this approach, I was able to control my work and plan my timing more effectively. It required me to be outcome-focused and accountable for the results, but it also provided a sense of empowerment and control over my schedule. I highly recommend this method to all of you. It allows you to plan your actions and manage your timing independently, leading to improved efficiency and productivity. It will increase your white space, definitely.

Let’s Break the Silence Around Menopause at Work

For too long, menopause has been treated as a private issue, when it is clearly a workplace one too. Our global Menopause Experience and Attitudes Study, covering 13,800 respondents across six countries, shows just how widespread the impact is:
- Over a third of people going through menopause experience some kind of negative impact at work.
- 1 in 20 believe they’ve lost out on promotions or pay rises.
- Many feel unable to talk to colleagues or managers.

This is a reality we can and must change.

That’s why I’m proud to support Astellas’ Pledge to Champion a Menopause-Inclusive Workplace. Through education, training, and open dialogue, we aim to create a culture where no one feels they have to suffer in silence.

This is about health, inclusion, and respect.

It’s also a reminder that leadership means listening, even when the topic is uncomfortable. It is especially important we listen then.

As I mentioned the other day, business leadership is essential for the realization of HR measures. In this article, I would like to introduce specific success stories.

先日お話しした通り、人事施策の実現にはビジネスリーダーのオーナーシップが欠かせません。今回は、その具体的な成功事例をご紹介したいと思います。

4年前、私は会社の価値観と行動規範を15年ぶりにアップデートしたいと考え、数名の役員に提案しましたが、その時は機が熟していなかったため、見事に玉砕しました。しかし、2年前から大きなビジネス部門での組織と業務プロセス変更があり、マインドセットと行動面の大きな改革が求められる時期が来ました。この波を捉え、昨年4月からビジネスリーダーと何度も議論を重ね、今年4月から新しいValues & Behaviors（V&B）を導入しました。これに至るまでに100バージョン以上の議論を行い、ビジネスリーダーの意見を徹底的に反映しました。

今回の導入では、ビジネスサイドにこの取り組みの必要性を感じてもらうことができたのが大きなポイントでした。ビジネスリーダーが自らV&Bについて語り、我々人事も各地へ赴き説明やQ&Aを行うなど、全社的に取り組みました。また、導入に際して世界中の66個のリーダーシップモデルを調査し、全てを廃止してV&Bに集中することを決めました。

実際に、ある経営会議の場面で人事に対する感謝のコメントがあったとき、ある役員が「これは人事がやったことではない、我々が主体だ」と言ってくれたことが心の底から嬉しかったです。人事の施策がビジネスリーダーによって推進され、成功を収めたことに大きなやりがいを感じています。これもひとえに同僚のリーダーや人事メンバーの協力のおかげです。

A recent conversation with people from the media gave me a chance to reflect on the evolving role of HR and the essence of human capital management.

Why do we need an HR department in the first place? My time at a global company challenged my assumptions more than any other experience. Before joining, I led HR for a Japanese subsidiary, where I naturally took the lead in talent and organizational discussions during regional and HQ reviews. It felt like a clear part of HR’s job. But at the company, the expectation was different. HR’s role was to coach and prepare business leaders—both regional / HQ and local—so they could lead meaningful conversations about talent and organization themselves.　At first, I thought, “It would be faster and more effective if I just did it myself.” But I soon realized: this is the point.

Talent and organizational matters are as fundamental to business as finance. As global leaders often say, “Finance in one hand, HR in the other.” Strong leaders take ownership of hiring, development, rewards, and culture. They don’t delegate these decisions and accountabilities entirely to HR—they shape them as part of their business strategy.

It may take more effort upfront, but unless business leaders truly own their talent and organizational challenges, HR initiatives risk being seen as disconnected or “just another program.” This isn’t about HR simply following business. It’s about HR identifying challenges, proposing solutions, and guiding leaders until they feel the challenge is their own.

I’d love to hear your thoughts. How is HR evolving in your organization?


人的資本経営の再考
最近のメディアとの会話は、人事の役割の進化と人的資本管理の本質について考える機会を与えてくれました。

そもそもなぜ人事部門が必要なのでしょうか?グローバル企業で過ごした時間は、他のどの経験よりも私の思い込みに挑戦しました。そちらへの入社前は日本法人の人事を率いていましたが、リージョンや本社のレビューでは、自然と人材や組織の議論を私が主導していました。それは人事部の仕事の明確な一部のように感じていました。しかし、その企業では人事への期待が私の想定とは違っていました。人事部の役割は、リージョン・本社と各国の両方のビジネスリーダーをコーチし、準備することで、人材と組織について有意義な会話を彼らが自分で主導できるようにすることでした。最初は「自分でやった方が早く、効果的だ」と思っていました。しかし、私はすぐに、これが重要ポイントであることに気づきました。

人材と組織の問題は、財務と同じくらいビジネスにとって基本的なものです。グローバルリーダーがよく言うように、「片手には財務、もう片方には人事」。強力なリーダーは、採用、能力開発、報酬、文化に責任を持ちます。これらの決定と説明責任を完全に人事部に委任するのではなく、ビジネス戦略の一部として形成します。

事前により多くの労力が必要になるかもしれませんが、ビジネスリーダーが自分のタレントと組織の課題を真に認識しない限り、人事イニシアチブはビジネスから分断された、または「単なる別のプログラム」と見なされるリスクがあります。ここで言いたいことは、人事部が単にビジネスをフォローするだけではありません。それは、人事部が課題を特定し、解決策を提案し、課題が自分のものであると感じるまでリーダーを導くことです。

I recently came across some fantastic insights on the importance of asking questions, particularly from Michael Marquardt and Bob Tiede's work – Leading with Questions. It reminded me of a tech giant CEO who always encouraged employees to ask questions, demonstrating an incredibly strong growth mindset. This practice has made me realize that asking questions is a key behavior that I often forget. I tend to jump straight to answers or recommendations, which isn't always the best approach.

Many exceptional leaders talk less and ask more questions, guiding their teams in the right direction. Even asking seemingly "stupid" questions can be beneficial, as it fosters a sense of psychological safety within the team. When leaders ask questions, it shows that it's okay for others to do the same. This approach is particularly useful when dealing with topics we're not entirely familiar with, as it allows us to delegate tasks more effectively.

It's essential to remember that asking questions shouldn't come across as accusatory. Instead, it requires good listening skills and can help resolve conflicts. Confident leaders aren't afraid to ask questions, as they understand that it doesn't make them appear weak. Some valuable questions to ask include: "How can I help you?", "What do you need to make it even better or quicker?", "What could we have done better?", "What would you do if you had the chance again?", "If we don't do this, what will happen?", and "What can be the best and worst-case scenarios?".

Ultimately, everything ties back to having a growth mindset for the future. I'm eager to continue improving my questioning skills and would love to hear your thoughts on this topic.

夏休みの前半に、徳岡晃一郎さんの「イノベーターシップ」を再度読み返してみました。少し前に「ライフシフト」という著作もあり、人生百年時代において「人生を生き切る」成長志向の重要性について述べられていたのが、私の成長志向（Growth mindset）にぴったりとフィットしました。老若問わず学び続けることが必要であり、特に「アウェイ体験・越境体験」の重要性や、常にWhyを考えつつ外の世界に自分を開くことが重要だとのこと。

また、徳岡さんご自身が59歳の時に「一人でも多くのミドル・シニアや若い人たちが、自分のキャリアを会社任せにせずプロアクティブに創造することで、人口減少下でも活力ある社会を創造する」というミッションを決められたと知り、非常に共感しました。徳岡さんの普段からの行動を裏付けるもので、「なるほど」と納得。ここがスタートポイントとなり、全ての徳岡さんの行動・活動が行われているのです。

さらに、ニトリの似鳥会長の言葉として、「リーダーとは10年先の目標と計画を立て、それを実現させる人」という言葉を紹介しており、最近よく言われる「バックキャスティング」の重要性にも触れていらっしゃいました。将来への恐れを低減させるためには、常に未来を考えることが大事だと、未来自身も私たちのステークホルダーだということでしょう。それにしても、徳岡さんの博識にはいつもながら本当に感心しました。

この本を読み返して、改めて自分の成長志向を再確認し、これからも学び続け、未来に向けた計画を立てていこうと決意を新たにしました。

To change our culture, we take down walls…literally.
 
At Astellas, we’ve been working hard to evolve our culture. Not just in what we say, but in how we lead, decide, and work together. Last month, we took a visible step forward: the top floor of our Tokyo HQ, once home to executive offices and the formal meeting space known as the “Decision Room,” has been fully transformed. No more private suites. No more separate executive floor.
 
In its place, we opened the One Astellas Floor, an open-plan space where senior leaders and employees now sit and collaborate side-by-side. Half of the floor is open plan, hot-desk seating for all colleagues, just like any other part of the office. This wasn’t just a renovation; it was a deliberate choice.
 
By stepping away from the Executive Floor and retiring the formal Decision Room, we’re moving beyond outdated symbols of hierarchy that can distance leaders from teams. In their place, we’re creating open spaces—both physically and culturally—where every colleague feels confident to speak up, share ideas, and shape our future together.
 
This change reflects the culture we’re building—flatter, more transparent, and more connected. It’s a reminder that leadership isn’t defined by square footage or seating charts, but by how accessible we are to the people we lead.
 
Sometimes, changing a culture starts by changing the floorplan!

This past weekend, the Pacific Northwest made history with a light rail train crossing a floating bridge for the very first time in history. 

As we crossed Lake Washington on the train’s inaugural ride, I thought about what this will mean for our Puget Sound employees. 

More than 40% of Microsoft’s employees in the region already commute by means other than driving. The access public transit provides is a game changer. Communities become more connected, day-to-day stress is lessened, and we all get to start, and end, our days a little less worn down by traffic. 

I had the honor of attending the celebration at the newly opened Judkins Park Station with my colleagues Teresa Hutson and Alice L. Jolla. In a personally meaningful moment, Senator Patty Murray pulled me aside and noted how great it was to see Microsoft represented by three women leaders.

As the largest employer on the Eastside, Microsoft has been involved in this project for more than 20 years. During the speaking program, King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci and others shared stories of the last 20 years and the tenacity, sweat equity, advocacy, and heart behind this achievement.

My dad was just featured in the Washington Post for a death penalty case from 1985… But the most important thing he’s ever taught me has nothing to do with the law. He is one of fewer than 20 attorneys qualified to take on capital cases in Utah and has decades of trial experience. He represents people in high-stakes life-or-death decisions. By any measure, he’s had an incredible career. But at my brother’s wedding, when he stood up to give a toast… He didn’t talk about success. He didn’t talk about ambition. He didn’t talk about winning. He shared just one piece of advice: “Spend time with the people you love.” ❤️ Then, holding back tears, he told a story. At his own wedding to my mom (they’re now happily divorced), the room was filled with parents, grandparents, and family. Now, 30+ years later, he looked around and said: "My sweet mom is the only one left" The lesson has stuck with me. Success matters, and it’s meaningful to climb the career ladder. But nothing matters more than the people you love and the time you get with them. My dad has taught me this time and time again. — Article in the comments if you’re curious about the case

January always sets the tone. It is a moment to define who we want to be in the year ahead – professionally and personally – and to anchor ourselves in purpose.

This year in Davos, AI was not just on the agenda – AI took center stage, and for good reason. Policymakers and business leaders across the globe are grappling with how AI is rewriting the rules of work, commerce, and daily life.

Yesterday, I had the honor of moderating an incredibly inspiring World Economic Forum session on AI and the future of work, with two visionary leaders Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach. Yesterday’s discussion made it clear that while AI continues to transform our world, it is our people – with their creativity, adaptability, and judgment – who are powering the future. 

We came away with three clear lessons leaders can use when empowering people to lead with AI:

1. Optimism over anxiety. The conversation is shifting, and employees are increasingly hopeful about what AI can do for them and their organizations. Success starts with leaders who champion and empower their teams to see challenges as opportunities. 

2. AI is for everyone. Universal adoption is key. AI should amplify every employee’s impact, regardless of their role. Commit to championing AI literacy in your organization, ensuring every person has the confidence and skills to thrive alongside AI tools. 

3. AI is the tool, but people are the power. Your people are the engine of transformation – fuel them. As leaders, we must invest in both cutting-edge tools and world-class training equally. When we do both, we do more than adopt AI – we lead the future.

Thank you to Judson and Carl for sharing your perspectives in such an insightful discussion. I look forward to helping shape the future of work we discussed – a future where AI amplifies and empowers what makes us uniquely human. #WEF26 Workday Microsoft

It’s a question that looms large for any business leader these days, but the stakes are even higher for those that manage massive workforces: As AI transforms the workplace, what happens to jobs and the people doing them?

On this episode of Where AI Works, host Matthew Bidwell speaks with Donna Morris, the chief people officer at Walmart, about what it means to introduce AI across one of the largest workforces on the planet; more than 2.1 million associates around the world. Morris explains the company’s “people-led, tech-powered” approach, where AI is used to augment employees rather than replace them. She also discusses the emergence of new roles like AI agent-builders, and explores the skills that matter most in an AI-driven workplace. While technical expertise is important, Morris argues that adaptability, communication, curiosity, and interpersonal skills will define the most successful employees in the years ahead. For leaders navigating this rapid change, the takeaway is simple: Invest in people, build new skills, and be sure to bring your workers along for the ride.

# March staff profile – Donna

Posted on: [26th March 2026](https://www.magrathea-telecom.co.uk/2026/03/), by Magrathea

This month we caught up with Donna, our Client Support & Accounts Specialist. Alongside supporting clients, she also takes the lead on all things financial.

We last featured Donna in 2021, so we thought it was the perfect time to revisit her role and see what a typical day looks like for her now.

#### Donna – tell us a bit about what you do at Magrathea?

I manage the finance team, where I am responsible for producing monthly reports and invoices. I also work within the client and sales support team which keeps things varied and means no two days are ever quite the same.

#### What do you enjoy most about your job?

It is hard to pick just one thing – what stands out most is the people and the culture. There’s a real sense of teamwork at Magrathea, the way everyone supports each other makes it an enjoyable place to be every day.

#### What are the most significant changes in the time you have been here?

Having been here for almost 17 years, I have seen a lot of change – thankfully all positive. The company has grown significantly, when I first started I could count the team on one hand, and now we have expanded far beyond that! The telecoms industry itself is also constantly evolving from a regulatory perspective, which keeps things interesting.

#### What advice would you give someone starting out in telecoms or finance?

Be open to learning, always ask plenty of questions and don’t underestimate how much you’ll pick up from people around you!

#### What’s your all-time favourite film, book, or TV show?!

It’s hard to choose just one! I love a mix of fantasy, action and adventure. Enid Blyton’s The Magic Faraway Tree books will always hold a special place from my childhood and I’m really looking forward to seeing them brought to life on the big screen.

#### And finally, how do you enjoy spending time outside of work?

We’re a skiing family, so we’re always planning our next slopes adventure. I also love stand-up paddleboarding by the coast, keeping active at our local tennis club (where I am also Treasurer) and exploring the countryside with our two dogs.

Thank you, Donna, for taking the time to catch up with us. It’s always a pleasure – and it’s great to hear more about your role and the work that keeps everything running smoothly, as well as what you enjoy outside of the office.

# Hy-Vee CEO shares tribute to Donna Tweeten

Tweeten, Hy-Vee’s first female president, was a central figure in shaping the retailer’s brand and national profile over a career spanning more than four decades.

April 10, 2026 . 12:13 PM

1 min read

WEST DES MOINES, Iowa — Hy-Vee Chairman and CEO Jeremy Gosch paid tribute to Donna Tweeten in a LinkedIn post, reflecting on her lasting impact on the company and the broader retail industry after her passing on April 8.

Tweeten, Hy-Vee’s first female president, was a central figure in shaping the retailer’s brand and national profile over a career spanning more than four decades. She joined the company in 2006 and served as chief marketing officer and later president, helping drive a series of high-profile partnerships and marketing initiatives that expanded Hy-Vee’s reach.

In his LinkedIn post, Gosch emphasized both his professional contributions and his personal influence across the organization.

“We are simply heartbroken by the sudden loss of Donna Tweeten. Not only was Donna a trailblazer across Hy-Vee and the retail industry, she was a true friend and mentor to many, myself included. Donna leaves behind a lasting legacy and will forever be remembered for her bold ideas, creative passion and commitment to excellence. We miss her deeply and words cannot express the sorrow that is being felt across our Hy-Vee family due to the impact she had on all of us,” he wrote.

Hy-Vee’s first female president, Donna Tweeten, dies at 63 | who13.com

DES MOINES, Iowa — Hy-Vee announced that Donna Tweeten, the company’s first female president, died following a battle with cancer.

Hy-Vee announced Thursday that Tweeten, age 63, had died April 8th following a battle with stage 4 pancreatic cancer. [Tweeten retired in January 2025](https://who13.com/news/iowa-news/first-female-president-of-hy-vee-drake-alum-retires/) but remained with Hy-Vee as a consultant up until her death.

Tweeten brought extensive advertising experience to Hy-Vee, having worked for firms including Davis Harrison Dion-Chicago and Anderson Communications, and played a significant role in helping the company reach national recognition. In 2006, Tweeten formally joined Hy-Vee as assistant vice president of communications and later held several positions, notably as the company’s chief marketing officer and later president.

The company says her leadership was instrumental in Hy-Vee becoming the first retailer to sign contracts with basketball star Caitlin Clark. Tweeten also secured major partnerships with other influential athletes, including Patrick Mahomes, Travis Kelce and Shawn Johnson East.

Jeremy Gosch, Chairman and CEO of Hy-Vee, expressed profound sadness over her loss. “We are simply heartbroken by the sudden loss of Donna Tweeten. Not only was Donna a trailblazer across Hy-Vee and the retail industry, she was a true friend and mentor to many, myself included.”

“Donna leaves behind a lasting legacy and will forever be remembered for her bold ideas, creative passion and commitment to excellence. We miss her deeply and words cannot express the sorrow that is being felt across our Hy-Vee family due to the impact she had on all of us.”

Throughout her career, Tweeten received national recognition across both the advertising and retail industries. She was named a Champion of Change by ADWEEK, honored as a Leading Women Forward recipient by Ad Age, and received the Mass Market Retailers’ Lifetime Achievement Award, among other accolades.

Tweeten is survived by her husband Alan and their five children, Carlie, Nick, Ben, Max and Ella, as well as her grandchildren.

Information regarding Tweeten’s funeral and service details has not yet been finalized. Those details are expected to be announced soon.

Some of the most meaningful conversations I’ve had as a leader have been with mothers sharing what they needed, and too often didn’t receive, during pregnancy and childbirth.

I've heard from women who wanted something simple but powerful: to feel supported, to be understood and to have someone by their side advocating for them.
 
Expanding access to doula support is one way we are working to make care more personal and more connected — helping mothers feel seen and supported before, during and after childbirth. This work is part of a bigger responsibility we have: to help make health care easier to navigate, more equitable and more affordable for the people we serve.
 
We know there is more work ahead. But listening, and turning what we hear into action, is how progress happens. Every mother deserves that support. Every family deserves a healthier start.

As Women’s History Month comes to a close, I’ve been taking a moment to reflect—not just on the month itself, but on the legacy we carry forward every day.
 
We stand on the shoulders of extraordinary women. Women like Marie Curie, who pushed the boundaries of science. Amelia Earhart, who redefined courage. Rosa Parks, who showed the quiet power of conviction. Katherine Johnson, whose brilliance helped launch humanity into space. Florence Nightingale, who transformed care through compassion and discipline. Mother Teresa, who embodied service. Jane Goodall, who taught us to listen more closely to the world around us.
 
And for me, this reflection is also deeply personal. I think about my mom—her resilience, her strength, and the example she set long before I understood what leadership really meant.
 
What connects all of these women isn’t just what they accomplished—it’s how they led. With purpose. With persistence. With a willingness to challenge what is and imagine what could be.
 
As leaders today, our responsibility is to carry that forward. To create space. To lift others. To lead in ways that make it easier for the next generation to rise even higher.
 
Women’s History Month may be ending, but the work—and the opportunity—continues.
 
Let’s keep going.

Raise your hand, opportunities are what you make them!

Today is National Intern Day. And right now, there are hundreds of incredibly bright and energetic young people wrapping up their summer at UnitedHealth Group. Drawn to our mission – to help people live healthier lives and help the health system work better for everyone – they’re gaining skills and experiences they’ll carry with them as they set out to do good in the world, here and beyond. 

My journey to health care started with an internship, too. I was fortunate to get a foot in the door of a Boston hospital. That summer, I was one of two interns working in the department. I was an undergrad. The other person was working on her master’s – and more than happy to brush all the grunt work my way. As it happens, she also helped me learn a most valuable lesson: Opportunities are what you make them.

One morning, our manager let us know there was a big meeting coming up. He asked if we could help. I raised my hand (she didn’t) and volunteered to stay late to put the briefing packets together, thinking maybe…just maybe...they’d let me come to the meeting. And they did. 

The next day, I showed up early in my red suit – my only suit – and found a seat. As the meeting got underway, one of our guests, the powerful Speaker of House for Massachusetts wrapped up his talk and asked if there were any questions. I took a deep breath, raised my hand and asked my question. Apparently, I made an impression. Because months later, he called the hospital. He was looking for someone to help him put together some focus groups and asked our boss, “what about that lady in the red suit?”
 
The rest of my career unfolded from there. 

If I hadn’t been willing to skip happy hour and stand at the copy machine working the three-hole punch, I might never have met a mentor who helped open a door to HR, which led to another door into law school, which led to a door to technology, and then another back to health care. 

So, as the summer intern season comes to a close, I want to extend my deepest appreciation to our incredible interns – for showing up with such great energy, perspective and a genuine eagerness to learn. It’s been truly inspiring to watch you grow. Keep showing up, keep raising your hands and keep building your networks, because you never know what opportunity will come your way. And remember this advice my mentor shared with me: “Be seen. Be heard. Be memorable.”

A few days after Valentine’s Day, I was reminded that “heart” isn’t just a symbol for love but for life. ❤️🧡

I was grateful to join the Heart-to-Heart event organized by our LEAD (Leading Employees of African Descent) employee resource group in observance of Black History Month and American Heart Month, raising awareness of chronic heart health within the Black community.

According to the American Heart Association, cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death for African Americans, with nearly 60% of Black adults (aged 20+) living with some form of CVD. During the session, our medical director Dr. Cara Pensabene, MD shared that prevention and management of cardiovascular disease start with awareness and access. Wellness benefits, like what we offer at Mastercard, support the mind, body, financial, and social well-being of our people. These are not “nice to have”; they reflect how we empower our employees to thrive, embracing flexibility and anchoring our culture in purpose and growth opportunities.

One key takeaway for me was this: even with full calendars, we have to be intentional about making time for self-care and focusing on what truly makes a difference. For me, that means moving more. I encourage you to prioritize your health and help spread awareness too.

#BlackHistoryMonth #AmericanHeartMonth #Wellbeing #WeAreMastercard

I’ve been reflecting on the theme of May’s #MentalHealthAwarenessMonth: Turn awareness into action.

Mental health can be hard to talk about, especially at work. But the more we avoid the topic, the more we miss the chance to lead with empathy and impact. Here are three things I’m focusing on, and I invite you to join me:

1. Pause and listen. Not every conversation needs a fix. But every person should feel seen and heard.

2. Be ready to point to support. I’ve had teammates open up about burnout, caregiving stress or feeling overwhelmed. I may not have had all the answers, but I could connect them to the breadth of mental health and well-being resources at AbbVie that helped.

3. Speak up. The more leaders talk openly about mental health, the more we normalize it and create a workplace where people feel comfortable asking for support.

Mental health awareness matters. And it’s what we do with it that drives change.

In a recent conversation with one of our Business Resource Groups, I was asked about strategies for moving into #leadership roles and it made me reflect on the important distinction between being managed and being mentored.

Both are essential – managers help us succeed where we are, mentors help us prepare for what’s next.

Great managers build performance. They set clear goals, coach through challenges, hold people accountable and remove barriers to team success. 

Great mentors build perspective. They help you zoom out – think strategically about your growth, test ideas, and explore what’s next. A strong mentor challenges your assumptions and helps you see possibilities you might not see yourself. 

If you are aspiring to lead, or even just accelerate your own development, here’s where you can start:

– Find a mentor who checks the right boxes.
 □ Has the skills, judgment or influence you want to build
 □ Is known for developing others and consistently leading high-performing teams
 □ Will offer honest feedback, including the tough truths to push and support you
 □ Sits outside your reporting line to allow more freedom for curiosity and candid exploration

– Use the time with your mentor to discuss lessons learned from their experiences, both successes and setbacks, as well as what you’re currently experiencing. 

– Engage your manager in open conversation about your goals and how to create stretch opportunities.

– Pair your mentor’s perspective with your manager’s coaching for greatest impact.

And if you already lead, be both – a strong manager who develops people today, and a mentor who invests in the leaders of tomorrow. Results always matter, but the greatest legacy is leaving behind those truly ready to lead.

– Put the Wrench Down: Why ROI Starts with People – 
  
There’s a fine line between what we can do and what we should do. I learned that the hard way—not in the office, but under my kitchen sink on a Saturday morning.

With a wrench in hand and YouTube at my side, I was determined to fix a stubborn hot water valve. But I realized something: sure, I could try. But at what cost? A flooded kitchen? Hours wasted? Instead, I called a plumber.

That small moment reminded me of something far bigger—the curse of competence. Just because we’re capable doesn’t mean it’s the best use of our time, energy or expertise.

In #HR, this shows up everywhere. We tell ourselves, “It’s easier if I just do it myself.” 

But real impact comes when we invest in the right skills, empower others and align work where it belongs—whether that’s business partners driving outcomes, specialized experts elevating the function or colleague self-service.

Over my 30+ years in HR, I’ve seen our profession transform from administrators to business enablers. The greatest #ROI isn’t in doing everything ourselves—it’s in unlocking the potential of people and maximizing efficiency.

Sometimes the smartest move is to put the wrench down. Because when we stop trying to do it all, we create space for growth, innovation and real returns—on skills, on people and on business results.

#strategicHR #HReffectiveness

September always feels like a reset – a reminder that none of us are ever too senior, too experienced or too established to keep learning. One of the most powerful, and sometimes overlooked, ways to grow is through #apprenticeship. 

At Thermo Fisher Scientific, we view apprenticeship as more than mentoring. It’s a two-way exchange between expert and learner, where both are developing, not just delivering. It’s a mutual investment built on trust, feedback and real-time collaboration.

—  For the expert, apprenticeship means sharing your thought process, creating scaffolds that empower independence, and coaching through real challenges – knowing when to step back so others can step up.
—  For the apprentice, it’s about watching closely, asking questions, articulating your reasoning and taking ownership of your growth. Over time, that practice builds both confidence and capability.

When done well, apprenticeship doesn’t just shape individuals – it builds a culture where learning is continuous, feedback is natural and teaching is everyone’s responsibility. That’s the kind of culture I want to be part of.

Looking back, I’ve been fortunate to experience both sides. I’ve learned the mechanics of a balance sheet from a former CFO and the basics of plumbing from my dad. Both shaped how I think, work and lead. And in turn, being able to teach others those same lessons has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career – and my life.

As this new season begins, I invite you to reflect: What are you learning? Who are you teaching? And how can we each show up as both expert and apprentice?

Here’s to learning, always – together.

We all remember our first internship or job out of college. 

For me, it was my first career job with a local plastics company in rural South Carolina. 

I had a lot to learn to effectively do that HR job, but a business leader saw potential in me and she helped me make the most of that experience. 

Over the course of my career in HR, I have found internships and other early talent roles to be very similar – a lot of raw talent and enthusiasm that just requires direction and thoughtful boundaries.   

So to all the recent grads starting their first career jobs this summer, or current students settling into their internships, I wanted to share some tips I wish I knew back then to make that development experience even stronger.  

 – Maximize your experience: Approach every task with enthusiasm and initiative. Your proactive attitude will not only enhance your experience but also demonstrate your potential to take on greater responsibilities. By treating every moment as a learning opportunity, the knowledge and skills you gain now will help build the foundation for your future success.

 – See the need, meet the need: With fresh eyes, you will see countless opportunities for improvement all around. Your perspectives can also help bring new solutions to a challenging problem. Think about the skills and experiences you bring and work with your manager to make a list of quick wins where you can have high impact. 

 – Be patient: Building skills and capabilities takes time – often longer than you think. When you consider the time it takes to understand the organization, build trust with stakeholders, and deliver on the responsibilities of your role, the growth happens on the journey – not in reaching the finish line. Focus on what experiences you need in the current role to prepare you for the next.   

And to all our interns and early talent colleagues here at Thermo Fisher Scientific, welcome to the team and go be great! 

Leaders – what is one thing you wish you knew when you were sitting in their seats?

Regardless of your job, just about all of us can agree that we want to bring our best selves to it each day. The same goes for our lives outside of work and those who depend on us. 

So during this #MentalHealthAwarenessMonth, it is important to remind ourselves that being at our best requires continued investment – including in our #mentalhealth. 

As someone who has experienced all areas of the circle of life recently, it is a timely topic for me so I wanted to share some simple ways we can take better care of ourselves and foster stronger work environments for everyone. 

 – Conduct a self check-in: This article https://lnkd.in/e76i-qWt provides some great ideas for questions to ask ourselves and assess how we are doing.
 – Ask for help: Those around you may not know what you are experiencing unless you tell them. Plus, when we ask for help, it can help others feel more confident doing the same. 
 – Prioritize your day: With finite hours in the day, prioritizing for impact can help maintain a sense of control and manage stress.
 – Practice self-care: Set aside time for activities that rejuvenate you, whether it is exercising, time outdoors, pursuing a hobby, or in my case – spending time with family. 
 – Get involved in your community: Volunteerism is proven to reduce stress and increase happy, positive feelings through the release of dopamine.

Wherever you are on your own mental health journey, let’s take at least one positive step in May together. Our families, coworkers, customers and communities will only be stronger as a result.
