Renminbi (RMB) usage is expanding across trade settlement, funding and capital markets, reshaping how corporates think about currency strategy. 

As a cross-border Bank, Standard Chartered sits at the intersection of where this shift is happening — across Greater China, ASEAN, the Middle East, Africa and beyond. We've been present on the ground in these markets for decades, building the relationships, the expertise and the infrastructure that allow us to connect clients to opportunity across the corridors that matter most.

That's why we've published Renminbi in Motion for Corporates — a report that moves beyond the macro narrative to where it really matters for our clients: funding flexibility, payments resilience, liquidity management, and FX alignment in an increasingly multipolar financial system.

Here's the context that makes it essential reading right now. China represents roughly 15% of global trade, yet the RMB accounts for less than 3.1% of global payments and just 1.9% of global reserves. That structural gap is narrowing, and the drivers this time are durable — rooted in real-economy demand rather than short-term policy cycles.

The infrastructure to support this is firmly in place, liquidity pools are deepening, and onshore and offshore markets are becoming increasingly connected. For corporates with China-linked exposure, this is no longer a theoretical conversation — your supply chains, procurement flows and revenue streams are already embedded in Asia-centred trade networks, whether or not your treasury framework has caught up.

Helping our clients navigate exactly that kind of complexity — with the expertise, the network and the long-term commitment to the markets where they operate — is what Standard Chartered is here to do.

I’ve been reflecting on how quickly geopolitical developments move from headlines to markets and real economic trade‑offs. In a recent conversation on our podcast, Standard Chartered's Eric Robertsen and Madhur Jha explored a key question - is the oil shock arising from the Middle East conflict more likely to fuel inflation pressures, or deepen growth concerns? They also unpacked how the Strait of Hormuz closure is affecting not just energy supplies, but other critical sectors, and what this means across regions, economies, and asset classes. 
 
What we’re seeing right now feels less like a single event and more like a multi‑step adjustment. Even if there is de‑escalation, it may not follow a smooth or predictable path. Ongoing uncertainty around key routes like the Strait of Hormuz matters, not just for oil prices, but for the wider global economy. 
 
A few patterns stand out. First, this is about more than energy prices. Oil and LNG are the most visible channels, but the Middle East is deeply embedded in global supply chains. Disruption can extend into petrochemicals, with knock‑on effects across multiple sectors. Where infrastructure has been damaged, especially LNG facilities, the economic impact can last for years. 
 
Second, markets are reacting through an inflation lens, but growth risks sit just behind it. Energy prices tend to hit inflation expectations quickly, and we’ve seen a shift away from expected rate cuts in some markets. History suggests that when price shocks persist, there is a bigger hit to growth that unfolds gradually over several quarters rather than all at once. 
 
Third, diversification is proving more challenging than expected.  Some traditional safe havens assets have not behaved as they typically do, which complicates risk management and portfolio construction. In this environment, liquidity and judgement matter as much as models. 
 
For me, the key takeaway is a familiar one. Periods like this reward clarity of thinking and patience. Not every signal deserves an immediate response. For businesses (and leaders), this is a reminder that steady long‑term thinking is a competitive advantage when uncertainty rises.

AI is reshaping business outcomes across the entire value chain – from customer services and marketing, to operations, finance and supply chains. Treasury management is no exception, though perhaps not in the way many expect.

I’ve been reflecting on how AI is showing up in day-to-day decision-making, not just in theory but in practice. This conversation with my colleague, Thomas Kikis, Head of Markets, US & Americas at Standard Chartered, offers a compelling window into that reality. 

In treasury management, AI is clearly improving cash flow forecasting, liquidity visibility, and the precision of hedging decisions - particularly in complex, data-fragmented environments like emerging markets. Yet what stood out to me most is a pattern we are seeing across the organisation: the constraint is rarely the technology itself. It is how we apply human judgement to the insights it generates. 

More data, more models, and more signals do not necessarily simplify decisions. In many ways, they increase the premium on human context, interpretation, and accountability.

It’s a reminder that transformation isn’t just about the “hardware” - the models, tools, and infrastructure - but the “software”: how we think, decide, and lead differently in response.

The real value of AI isn’t in replacing judgment, but in sharpening it. That balance between machine-led precision and human-led accountability is where the most meaningful transformation takes shape. 

The podcast is worth a listen for anyone thinking about how AI moves from capability to real-world impact.

This week marks Neurodiversity Awareness Week, a timely reminder of how important it is to recognise that we all work, think, learn, and process information in different ways. 
 
To mark the week, we gathered colleagues across our markets to discuss a fundamental truth: creating a culture where people of all abilities thrive shouldn’t be complex, and it doesn’t require each of us to become an expert in every type of disability – it simply requires us to be curious and open minded. 

As the Global Sponsor of the Standard Chartered Ability Colleague Community, I was thrilled to join Disha Mehta and Ollie Thorn alongside colleagues in London to discuss how the experience of visible and invisible disability can impact leadership. My key takeaways from our session:

​1️⃣ Stop fixing humans, start fixing environments - we spend too much time trying to make people fit a mold. Real change happens when we design environments that accommodate everyone from the start.

​2️⃣ The Power of Lived Experience - having the “ingredients” for a good culture isn't enough. We must amplify the voices of those with diverse lived experiences. Their stories are the catalysts for true transformation.

​3️⃣ Create Safe Spaces - when we build forums where people can share openly, we bridge the gap between "initiative" and "impact."

​4️⃣ The Long Game - we often overestimate what we can do in one year, but underestimate what we can accomplish in ten. Changing the world doesn't happen overnight, but it starts with the questions we ask today.

​Our discussion reinforced my view that inclusion isn't a box to check; it's a muscle we build every day by active listening and driving small impactful change with consistency.

When International Women's Day comes around, I find myself reflecting on a simple but powerful truth: progress is never accidental. It’s the result of deliberate choices, sustained commitment, and — critically — the courage to be transparent about where we still fall short.
 
IWD is a timely reminder that equality is not a destination. It is a discipline and at Standard Chartered, this discipline runs through everything we do — for our colleagues, our clients, and our communities.
 
Since signing the Women in Finance Charter in 2016, we have increased women's representation in senior leadership from 25% to over 33%. We introduced equalised parental leave of at least 20 weeks globally; became one of the first global institutions to offer menopause-related medical cover; and in last year, while many others pulled back on flexible working, we leaned in — trusting our people and their leaders to find what works. Our Inclusion Index stands at over 80%, reflecting a culture where colleagues feel heard, valued, and empowered.
 
Through SC WIN — our Women's International Network — we have committed to USD 1 billion in financing for women-led businesses globally by 2028. Since launching in 2022, the programme has already delivered USD540 million to women entrepreneurs across seven markets.
 
And through the Standard Chartered Foundation, programmes such Goal, Futuremakers, and Women in Tech continue to create pathways for young women — reaching hundreds of thousands of girls and young women across more than 20 countries with life skills, financial literacy, mentoring, and seed funding.
 
I am proud of what we have built. But I am equally honest about what remains. According to McKinsey & Company, globally women are underrepresented at every stage of the corporate pipeline and continue to be promoted to management roles in smaller numbers. The structural barriers — from discriminatory norms to funding gaps — are real and persistent.
 
That is why this work is not a programme. It is not a campaign. It is how we do business. Because when women thrive — in boardrooms, in businesses, in communities — everyone benefits. That is not aspiration. That is evidence.
 
Happy International Women's Day to the extraordinary women across our network — and to every ally who understands that equality is not a zero-sum game.

Recently I sat down with Brant Carson and Ishaan Seth from McKinsey & Company to share my reflections on what it really takes to drive lasting transformation — and why so often leaning towards conventional wisdom leaves transformation programmes missing the mark.
 
Transformation is one of the most overused words in business. Too often it describes a change programme with a start and end date, but real transformation requires you to hardwire new ways of working into how an organisation operates — not just declare them from the top. This is why the relationship between what I call the software, and hardware matters so much.
 
Most organisations instinctively reach for the hardware — the structural investments, the new processes, the governance mechanisms. And these matter, but the harder, and far too often underweighted, work is the software - the mindset shifts, the behavioural changes and the leadership culture that must carry the whole agenda. 
 
At Standard Chartered, the most powerful shift came when we stopped treating these as separate workstreams and started designing them together — mapping our processes, establishing clear accountability, and only then asking how to hardwire a culture of client centricity and innovation into the daily flow of work.
 
During the interview we also discussed the topic of AI, and my views that the barriers to adoption at scale are not technical in nature, but rather skills, leadership, and cultural challenges. The organisations that will lead in the race to capitalise on AI investments are those that build an environment where people engage with these tools confidently in the flow of their work, where human capabilities are augmented, not replaced by machines. As leaders, the responsibility to navigate this sits squarely with us.

Day 3 at Davos is always reserved for a breakfast roundtable I host in our offices on everything to do with Transformation, AI (clearly the topic of the moment!) and Skills. We discussed the progress we’ve seen in the AI space over the last year, the impact this is having on business strategies and how the most forward-thinking businesses are preparing their workforces for an AI-augmented world. A special thanks to Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Ravin Jesuthasan, CFA, FRSA, Katy George for their unique insights, alongside the other industry leaders who joined us at our Standard Chartered Pavilion. 

The discussions focussed on different approaches leaders are taking to augment or re-write business practices in an AI driven world, and the urgent need to reshape skill-building paths to support young professionals entering a rapidly shifting workforce. 

My key takeaways:
1️⃣ AI is now mission-critical infrastructure. It has moved beyond ‘pilot stage’ for companies worldwide (a panellist referred to it as ‘death of the use case’). Large firms are embedding AI deeply across the entire value chain – from customer service and marketing, to operations, finance and supply chains. For me it was great to see that this year, of all years, we are at a unique inflection point where technology, business strategy (and the transformation that underpins it) and people are not separate priorities but an integrated conversation. 

2️⃣ The true opportunity lies in weaving AI into broader transformation. AI cannot be viewed as just a technology project - it must be a strategic accelerant. This will enable leaders to re-architect customer journeys, streamline processes, and unlock new business models. Data reveals that companies taking this integrated approach are seeing revenue growth at double the rate of those who have yet to embed AI into their strategy and operations. As a panellist said - we need to lead with work not tech! 

3️⃣ Prioritising skills development so people can work alongside AI is key. Leaders should focus on how we prepare the workforce to thrive alongside AI and utilise it to augment and enhance people’s productivity. We discussed the shift away from traditional mindset of ‘self-directed learning’ to taking a more prescriptive approach to skill building – the need to remove optionality for our workforces to drive true skill building at scale.

Ultimately businesses that demonstrate conviction and courage will differentiate themselves in the long run. A big thank you to the panellists and industry leaders who joined me for the rich conversation. Also thank you to Diane Brady, Lisa Stevens, and Marco Amitrano from Bloomberg Live , PwC, Fortune and Aon for inviting me to their discussions during the day. 
 
#futureofwork #davos2026 #wef26 #artificialintelligence

Day 2 at Davos and it was great to join two thought-provoking panels hosted by McKinsey & Company, diving into two areas that are pivotal for any organisation wanting to stay future-ready: Artificial Intelligence and Workforce Health.
 
What stood out in our discussions were three critical priorities for leaders navigating today’s landscape:
1️⃣ Success in the AI era is not just about deploying new tools – it’s about transforming how organisations operate. The real difference will come from rewiring operating models, talent strategies, and governance to ensure that AI is embedded across workflows for real, measurable impact.
2️⃣ Health is and will remains a strategic investment with outsized returns. Workforce health – spanning brain, metabolic, and women’s health – is a foundational driver of productivity and resilience. Research highlights that employees with higher wellbeing are up to 13% more productive, and organisations that embed wellbeing practices are far more likely to achieve their objectives. Prioritising wellbeing is one of the best investments we can make, especially as we build the judgement and agility needed in an AI-powered world.
3️⃣ Leaders must lead by example. For real change, leaders need to personally champion both AI adoption and holistic wellbeing. This means supporting development, promoting tools (a plug for our brand-new AI wellbeing agent), and demonstrating a commitment to health in our own daily practices. Only by placing these values at the core of a company's culture can we build organisations where people truly thrive.
 
Huge thanks to Ishaan Seth, Kate Smaje and Lucy Perez for inviting me along to your discussions, and to my fellow panellists May Habib, Andrew McAfee, Daniel Skovronsky and Regina Dugan for such brilliant conversations.
 
It was also great to catch-up with many of clients and partners at our very own Standard Chartered evening reception!

I am pleased to share Standard Chartered Foundation’s new briefing, Adapting to the Changing Aid Landscape.

The findings highlight a stark reality; the world faces a US$4.3 trillion annual financing gap to meet the Sustainable Development Goals and potential aid cuts risk jeopardising access to education for roughly 68 million children worldwide. 

At the same time the landscape is shifting in ways that open up new possibilities, with remittances now exceeding both FDI and ODA combined, reaching US$685 billion- a reminder that the most powerful flows shaping development are not the ones traditionally labelled “aid.” 

This is where corporate philanthropy sits at the intersection of purpose, capital and capability. The document highlights three opportunities for businesses to play a leadership role in this space:

1️⃣ Collaborate and co-invest: Work with development banks, philanthropies and governments to unlock blended finance, de-risk innovation and draw in private capital.
2️⃣ Apply core business strengths: Use corporate expertise, not just grant budgets, to build inclusive, market-linked models that can scale sustainably.
3️⃣ Shift power locally: Back locally led organisations and flexible funding models that respond to rapidly changing realities on the ground.

As a Trustee of the Standard Chartered Foundation, I have seen first-hand how this approach can be a powerful catalyst. When we leverage our unique business capabilities to unlock meaningful, lasting change.

I was delighted to close the event by discussing topics close to my heart: the evolving nature of work and the skills that will shape the future of Banking, alongside the power of networks as a source of continuous learning and finding ‘joy’ at work! We discussed the importance of owning our own development journeys and having the courage to lean into new - and sometimes uncomfortable - opportunities when they arise through the course of our careers. 

As always it was super energising to spend time with an incredibly talented cohort, and I feel confident that our graduates will play a pivotal role in driving the success of the Bank as they move on to the next stage of their career journey with us.

I wish all of them the very best…

I was delighted to join Ravin Jesuthasan, CFA, FRSA in a fireside chat alongside Amy Edmondson and Merete Hverven at the Thinkers50 event in London. It was great to be with a room full of leaders who are at the heart of driving transformational change and navigating a complex organisational and societal landscape. 

Our discussion focussed on humanising change and explored how companies need to strike the balance between the growth and efficiency opportunities offered in this new age, with a real focus on safeguarding
organisational and societal sustainability. 
 
As a long-term fan – I continue to be inspired by Amy’s comments on psychological safety and our innately human ability to learn through failure. I particularly love the distinction she makes between mistakes and intelligent failures - with the latter being a critical part of learning, innovation, and growth. 
 
This session was a real reminder to me that despite the exponential rate of technological innovation and change, deeply human traits such as learning agility, curiosity and trust will always remain crucial to the success of teams and companies.   
 
A special thank you to Ravin for bringing this inspirational group together for such an engaging evening. 
 
#Thinkers50 #Leadership

There are few events that are as energising as the One Young World annual gathering and I was delighted to be back at One Young World - Munich 2025, attended by over 2,000 young leaders and changemakers from 196 countries. The atmosphere was absolutely electrifying! 
 
I spoke about one of the most important topics shaping our future – the evolving relationship between humans and AI. During my session, I emphasised that whilst AI will undoubtedly transform the way we work, it will not replace the uniquely human qualities that define us – empathy, curiosity, creativity and emotional intelligence. Instead, it will take away repetitive tasks, giving us more space to focus on innovation, connection and purpose.  
 
The key for all of us is to keep learning – continuously investing in ourselves to stay ahead, stay relevant and thrive in the new world of work. Lifelong learning is no longer optional; it is essential. 

Spending time with our Standard Chartered delegation was a real highlight. It comprised 10 talented colleagues and 20 Next Gen participants from our Priority Private and Private Banking clients. The passion and commitment that our delegation, and all the other attendees I met, have for building a better future left me feeling incredibly optimistic.  
 
Moments like this remind me why I love what I do – being part of a community that believes in the power of people, technology, and purpose to create lasting impact. A huge thank you to Kate Robertson for inviting me back.  
 
#FutureOfWork #AI

Last week, Standard Chartered Global Private Bank hosted the 2025 Global Families Network forum in Dubai. This exclusive, closed-door event, now in its second year brought together ultra-high-net-worth families from over 31 markets globally, underscoring our role as a strategic partner and global connector. 

Focussed on supporting our clients’ holistic needs, the event bought together a host of experts, to engage in discussions on the future of wealth, leadership, and legacy.

The forum was aligned with the insights from our latest report, “The Great Repositioning” (link in comments), which focused on four key themes: navigating geopolitical instability, adapting to digital disruption, managing profound social change and rethinking traditional approaches to wealth preservation. 
 
It’s inspiring to see how family businesses are creating resilience as they rethink how to build, protect, and pass on their wealth. It is also great to see the role we are playing in supporting our clients on their wealth journey, leveraging our extensive network across markets and deep local expertise to help them achieve their aspirations.
 
My thanks and congratulations to Raymond Ang, Eva Ang, and all of your teams for bringing this diverse group together – I’m already excited to be back with you all at next year’s forum.

Today we mark Purple Tuesday, a day that holds personal meaning for me as Standard Chartered’s Global Sponsor of our Ability Colleague Community.
 
My learning journey in this space started years ago in Kenya when a visually impaired colleague shared her experience on the barriers she faced completing the Bank’s online learning. She was unable to invest in her development without the assistance of another colleague to help her navigate the online learning courses. That conversation led to a decision to ensure that all the learning we deliver in the Bank is fully accessible. That moment was a reminder to me that small, thoughtful changes can make a significant difference in driving greater inclusion in the workplace. 
 
Since then, I’ve had the privilege of listening to more colleagues share their lived experiences of disability – both visible and invisible – as well as those who care for loved ones with a disability. Their honesty, resilience, and creativity have shaped how I think about leadership and reminded me that true progress begins with empathy and action. 
 
Building on these insights, we’ve continued to enable inclusion in practical ways. From introducing workplace adjustments and assistive technology for colleagues, to sign language services for clients in India and Taiwan, I’ve seen firsthand how these steps can transform everyday experiences. 
 
That’s why I’m especially proud that Standard Chartered is Purple Tuesday’s global lead sponsor for the fourth consecutive year. This partnership reflects our ongoing commitment to making accessibility and inclusion part of how we work every day. While there’s more to do, I believe that when we listen, learn and lead with intention, we create a culture where everyone has opportunities to thrive. 
 
#PurpleTuesday #Inclusion

Sometimes the blazer just has to feel too big at first…

This morning my youngest started senior school. His hand-me-down blazer from his big brother is at least a size too big, sleeves past his hands, shoulders a little too wide, but he wore it proudly even if I can tell he’s a bit anxious about what lies ahead. 

And it struck me that’s exactly how growth feels. Whether it’s starting a new role, taking on more responsibility, or stepping up as a leader, we rarely feel like the blazer fits on day one. It feels oversized, a little daunting, maybe even uncomfortable.

But over time, with encouragement, support and experience, we grow into it. Eventually, what once felt far too big becomes second nature.

At Man Group, we talk about high performance and culture but really, it’s about creating the kind of environment where people feel safe enough to try, supported enough to stumble, and encouraged enough to keep going until the blazer fits.

As leaders, our job isn’t to tailor the blazer to fit perfectly on day one. It’s to help people grow into it.

Father’s Day lands differently for all of us.

My dad left when I was six weeks old. I didn’t grow up with a father figure, and the little I did know of him didn’t leave much to admire. For a long time, this day felt like something I’d been left out of.

Now, watching my husband, who leads our home with calm, humour, and boundless love for our two boys, I feel a different kind of emotion. Gratitude. Pride. Hope. He’s rewritten the story for our family, and for that I’ll always be thankful.

But I know not everyone feels that way today.

Father’s Day can be joyful, painful, complex, or just quietly hard. And that’s the thing - we don’t always know what someone else is carrying. A cheerful message might land perfectly for one person and ache for another.

As colleagues and leaders, this is a simple but powerful reminder: inclusion means remembering not everyone shares the same story. It means creating space for people to show up as they are, not just how we expect them to be.

So here’s to the brilliant dads, the stepdads, the mums doing both jobs, the father figures, and to those feeling loss or absence today.

And to my husband, thank you for being the kind of dad I wish I’d had.

Today is Social Mobility Day and it’s prompted me to reflect on both where I started in life and where I stand today.

I grew up in a single-parent family in South Wales. We lived on benefits and I had free school meals. My mum was unemployed for much of my childhood as she cared for her own parents. The word ‘mobility’ wasn’t one we used, but I knew I wanted something different and I worked hard to get there.

Fast forward to today, and I’m fortunate to lead people strategy at Man Group, a global investment firm. I’ve built a career I’m so very proud of, raised two amazing boys with my husband, and have choices my younger self could never have imagined.

And yet… my children now grow up with the safety net I never had: the bank of mum and dad, a strong network, and all the access that brings. It’s something I think about a lot, especially on days like today.

This morning, I joined a breakfast with the brilliant Dr Eliza Filby, whose insights on generational shifts and the future of wealth really struck a chord. Her reflections on how aspiration and identity are changing, and how wealth inequality is reshaping opportunity, sparked a conversation that’s stayed with me all day. Thank you, Eliza, for your sharp thinking and honesty.

Later this afternoon, I had the privilege of hosting a fireside chat with Sarah Legg, one of our NEDs at Man Group. Sarah’s story, from working-class roots to boardroom leadership, is inspiring and grounded in real life experience. Together, we explored how social mobility isn’t just about career progression anymore. It’s about belonging, building security, and navigating a world where opportunity feels increasingly uneven.

At Man Group, we’re working hard to change that. Through our Paving the Way programme, our people volunteer in schools and universities, offer mentoring, host insight days, and open up real access to careers in finance for those who might otherwise be shut out. It’s one of the ways we’re trying to widen the door, not just hold it open.

Talent is everywhere. Opportunity isn’t.
Merit alone doesn’t level the playing field - access does.

On this Social Mobility Day, I’m thinking not just about how far I’ve come, but about how we keep making the journey easier for others.  It’s getting harder not easier but it really matters.  It’s something we all need to care about, deeply.

Both my boys have moderate to severe hearing loss. I still remember when we found out. That quiet moment of devastation. The tears. The mourning for all the things I thought they wouldn’t be able to do.

But the truth is, the only real limitation was in my mind. 

They’ve taught me that deafness isn’t about silence. It’s about resilience, creativity and connection, just in different forms. I’m writing this from the side of a cricket pitch, watching my youngest play, surrounded by teammates who’ve never made his hearing loss a thing. They just get on with the game.

Children can be incredibly inclusive. Naturally, instinctively. We could all learn a lot from that.

So this week, I’m thinking about what it really means to go beyond silence. To move past assumptions and towards understanding.

Because deaf kids, like mine, can do anything. And when we listen properly, we hear so much more.

Yesterday, I buried my Mam’s ashes.

It was quiet and simple. Full of love. A final act of goodbye that still doesn’t feel quite real.

Mam was strong, warm, and wonderfully no-nonsense. I like to think we were quite similar 😊. She always saw people – really saw them – and had a way of making you feel you mattered. I’ve thought about her a lot over the past few weeks, especially as I’ve watched so many people around me navigate their own moments of uncertainty. These really are unprecedented times in so many ways.

There’s tension and unease for people from all walks of life, not just the financial sector, but also the steel industry where I started my career. People are worried about the future, their financial security, their retirement options or how to lead in the face of so much unpredictability.

Grief and uncertainty often arrive together. Both unsettle us. Both ask us to sit with the unknown. And both can show up in unexpected ways: in withdrawal, distraction, or a feeling of being overwhelmed by even the smallest things.

As I head into the office today, I’m reminding myself of this. To be present. To be patient. To make space for what’s hard without rushing to fix it. To remember that people bring their whole selves to work – grief, doubt, worry and all.

If you’re carrying any of those things right now, I see you. You’re not alone.

And for those of us in leadership, there’s something really powerful we can do. We can slow down a bit. Check in, really listen, and show people they matter – not just for what they do, but for who they are. It doesn’t have to be grand or complicated. Often it’s the small, human moments that make the biggest difference.

And here’s the thing: when we help someone feel a bit less alone, we feel it too. That sense of connection, of shared humanity – it anchors us. It reminds us why what we do matters. And in the middle of all the noise and uncertainty, that can be a lifeline for all of us.

It was great to be part of this month's Sage TV Live. 

For those outside Sage, it’s our monthly internal live session where colleagues interview a leader in front of a live audience, creating space for open, honest conversation about what’s happening across the business.  

What I value most about these sessions is the chance to connect more directly, hearing what’s on people’s minds, taking questions, and having a real discussion about where we are and where we’re going. 

This time, we covered a few big themes:  

• How AI is changing the way we work and why building confidence and a willingness to learn really matters  
• The skills that will help all of us thrive as work continues to evolve  
• What it really means to bring customer empathy into everyday decisions 
• Our priorities as we close out H1 and look ahead to H2  

A big part of my role is making sure we’re creating the right environment for people to do their best work. And that starts with honest, transparent conversations like these.

Last week I spent time in India with our teams in Bangalore, my first visit back since 2007, and my first time there with Sage. 

It was great to connect with colleagues across the business, from engineering and product to our emerging talent and to hear directly about the work happening here. You can really feel the energy, ambition and opportunity ahead as we continue to grow as one. 

India plays such an important role in our global story, not just because of the scale, but because of the depth of talent and the impact teams here are having on what we build and how we grow. 

Bangalore has become a hub for technology and AI talent, and that curiosity and capability comes through in every conversation. But more than anything, it’s the people and culture that stood out, the openness, collaboration, pride in the work, and the impact our colleagues have both within Sage and in their communities. 

Trips like this are always a great reminder of what we’re building together. Thank you to everyone who took the time to share their work, ideas and experiences last week!

Last week was Neurodiversity Week, and it sparked some great conversations across Sage about how we make space for different ways of thinking at work. 

Many organisations, often unintentionally, still reward a fairly narrow style of contribution: thinking quickly, speaking confidently, and aligning fast. It works… but it also means we can miss valuable perspectives that don’t show up in that same way. 

Some of the most valuable insights I’ve seen don’t happen in the moment. They come later, from people who’ve had time to reflect, connect the dots, and really think things through. And when we make space for that, the quality of decisions improves. 

So maybe the question is less about getting everyone to contribute in the same way, and more about how we create the conditions for different thinking to shape outcomes. 

In reality, that often comes down to small things: 
💠  Giving people time to think before and after discussions 
💠  Making space for written input, not just verbal 
💠 Noticing whose perspective we haven’t heard yet 

As we move beyond Neurodiversity Week, that feels like the opportunity,   not just recognising difference, but actually designing for it. 

Because better thinking leads to better decisions.

I joined a panel on the evolving dynamic between the CPO, executive team and the board. With culture, succession and organisational risk rising up board agendas, the discussion really highlighted what true alignment at the top looks like. 

We explored:
•	How CPOs can become the board’s trusted voice on culture, succession and risk. 
•	Balancing transparency, politics and influence in today’s complex environment.

The discussion was a reminder of the power of collaboration and challenge in leadership. It’s inspiring to see how much impact a strong partnership between HR and the board can have on long-term value.

Continuing my interesting conversation with Sage early careers colleagues, discussing what it’s like to start out in your career and how your first roles can shape the way you work. We explored what it’s like to learn quickly on the job, adapt to different challenges, and experience the variety of work in a real team environment. 

I shared one piece of advice I wish I’d received earlier: don’t be afraid to speak up. It’s easy to feel like others know more than you, but sharing your perspective, even as someone just starting out, can add real value and help you grow professionally. 

If you’re at the beginning of your career, this video is a reminder that your ideas matter, and that being bold and curious can open doors.

Early careers aren’t just about the next step in someone’s journey, they’re vital to the future of our organisation.  

At Sage, we know that diversity of perspective drives innovation. Bringing in people at the start of their careers means fresh ideas, new ways of thinking, and challenges to established ways of working.   

It’s also about sustainability: investing in early careers ensures we’re building the leaders of tomorrow and creating an organisation that thrives across generations.  

I had the pleasure of talking with two of our exceptional early career colleagues, Sekeyna Abidi, Graduate Product Manager and Millie Storey, Customer Support Apprentice, about why this is so important. Their energy, ideas, and perspectives remind me every day why we must continue to support and nurture talent at the start of their journey.

Thrilled to see this recognition for Sage, being named Britain’s Most Admired Software & IT Services Company is a huge endorsement of our strategy, leadership, and the incredible people behind it. 

It’s a reminder that when we stay focused on our purpose, we can make work and business better for customers, colleagues and communities alike.

Yes, that’s me—#33—senior year. I didn’t know it then, but trying out for that team changed everything.
On my first day of high school, I remember the swirl of questions in my head:
 What classes should I take?
 Will I make new friends?
 What do I want to do when I grow up?

Spoiler: I didn’t have all the answers. But one of the most important decisions I made was trying something new—trying out for the basketball team. That single decision opened a door that shaped my high school experience and beyond.

Being part of my very first team—one that would go on to win a state championship—taught me lessons no textbook or training manual ever could. I learned that a collection of individual stars doesn’t make a team. Real success comes from showing up consistently, committing to each other, being coachable, and working toward something greater than yourself.

Coach Fujii fostered that mindset. He didn’t just build a winning team—he built a family.

That mindset made me a better student, a better teammate, and a better professional. And to this day, I carry those lessons with me—on and off the court.

If I could tell my younger self one thing, it would be:
 "You don’t need all the answers on Day One. Just be open to the experiences that help you grow."

Still learning, still growing—just not quite jumping as high.

AI is already more powerful than what most organizations are able to realize today.

This idea kept coming up at Lake Como last week in conversations with business leaders. The challenge is turning that potential into new ways of working, new skills, and real business impact. That was the focus of the SAP Italy Executive Summit, where more than 100 leaders came together to discuss how to build future-ready organizations in an AI-driven world.

In my conversations with Lavinia Spingardi, Carla Masperi, and Augusta Spinelli, we explored why so many companies still struggle to unlock AI at scale: Many are still trying to layer AI onto fragmented data landscapes, siloed processes, and legacy operating models. As a result, AI remains isolated in use cases instead of transforming how work actually gets done.

Organizations that move ahead take a different approach: they redesign workflows end-to-end, integrate AI directly into core processes, and clearly state where decisions are augmented by AI, and where accountability remains human.

During an interview with Giulia Cimpanelli for La Repubblica, another dynamic became very clear: many organizations are currently in the productivity dip of AI transformation. That dip exists because work is being rebuilt while results are not yet visible. People are learning new skills, roles are shifting, and processes are being redesigned at the same time. The critical mistake is to interpret this phase as failure. In reality, it’s where the real work happens – rebuilding skills, processes, and ways of working.
This is exactly the moment where leadership matters most. Being clear about direction, transparent about what’s changing, and giving people the space to learn and adapt, even when things feel less efficient at first.

Grateful for the conversations, the openness, and the shared ambition to not just adopt AI, but to truly turn it into value for business and people.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Thank you to Ricarda Engelmeier, Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. Horst Wildemann and everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful discussion.

Last week at the EU Skills Summit in Brussels, hosted by The Lisbon Council, I was honored to speak about a topic that sits at the heart of Europe’s future competitiveness:

The transition to a skills-based economy – accelerated by the rise of #AI.

At SAP, we see every day how AI is not just creating new jobs — it is reshaping existing roles, requiring a dynamic mix of technical expertise, learning agility, and human-centered skills. For me, they key lesson is clear: In this new reality, #skills are the true currency of growth, innovation, and resilience. Transitioning to a skills-based economy is not an option. It is a necessity if we want Europe to lead in AI, green technology, and digital innovation.

To meet this challenge, SAP is investing across all dimensions of people development. We collaborate with universities and educational institutions worldwide to equip our people with critical business and technology skills. 

Through initiatives such as Educate to Employ, which builds digital skills and opens career pathways for marginalised youth, and through partnerships with leading European university alliances like ENGAGE.EU as well as global efforts like Generation Unlimited, UNICEF’s worldwide platform, we are fostering stronger collaboration between education and industry.

True progress happens when business, education, and policy move forward together. That is why initiatives like the European Commission’s Union of Skills & STEM Education Strategic Plan are so important — and why SAP stands ready to support them with full commitment.

Thank you to Executive Vice-President Roxana Minzatu and the EU commission for the opportunity to contribute. Europe’s future strength will be measured by how boldly we invest in skills today. I am confident we can achieve this and make it happen together.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.


Bundesministerium für Bildung, Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend | DIW Berlin - German Institute for Economic Research

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

Der Übergang ins KI-Zeitalter ist mehr als nur eine technologische Evolution. KI wird die Arbeitswelt entscheidend verändern und neue Fähigkeiten fordern und fördern. Wir müssen dafür bei Bildung und Arbeit bestehende Muster durchbrechen und neue Wege gehen. Es gilt, die Menschen darauf vorzubereiten – angefangen bei der schulischen Ausbildung bis zu lebenslangem Lernen im beruflichen Umfeld und der Integration von KI in Arbeitsprozesse.

Als ein global führendes Unternehmen und einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland, sehen wir uns als Vordenker im Umgang mit KI. Wir ermutigen unsere Mitarbeitenden, ihre Kompetenzen ins KI-Zeitalter zu überführen, mit den neuen Technologien zu wachsen und diese mitzugestalten. Gleichzeitig legen wir in unserer Aus- und Weiterbildung Wert auf die Vermittlung grundlegender Fähigkeiten, wie etwa kritisches Denken, die Kernvoraussetzung für Entscheidungsfindung, Problemlösung und die Beurteilung von Informationen. Mit diesem umfassenden Skills-Ansatz sehen wir unsere Mitarbeitenden gut vorbereitet, um auch in Zeiten großer Technologieveränderungen für den Arbeitsmarkt langfristig relevant bleiben zu können.

Die von Siemens und weiteren Unternehmen ins Leben gerufene Initiative #Made4Germany ist ein vielversprechender Beitrag, um Deutschland nicht nur wirtschaftlich wieder ganz nach vorne zu bringen, sondern auch in den Bereichen Arbeit, Bildung und Soziales neue Impulse zu setzen. 

Ich bin überzeugt, dass uns dies gelingen kann – im Schulterschluss von Wirtschaft, Politik und Gesellschaft - wenn wir es gemeinsam und mit Zuversicht angehen!

Seit mehr als 175 Jahren glauben wir bei Siemens daran: Technologie entfaltet ihre volle Wirkung erst durch die Menschen, die sie gestalten und anwenden. Deshalb freue ich mich sehr, dass wir zum Start in den September wieder 1.700 Auszubildende und dual Studierende bei Siemens begrüßen durften. 🎓

#Bildung ist der Schlüssel zu Innovationskraft, nachhaltigem Fortschritt und der Zugehörigkeit zur Gesellschaft. Auch diese Generation junger Talente will eigenverantwortlich arbeiten, sich weiterentwickeln und Sinn stiften mit ihrer Tätigkeit. Deshalb fördern wir bei Siemens neben digitalen auch grundlegende Fähigkeiten wie kritisches Denken und Problemlösungskompetenz – für Menschen, die #Wandel aktiv gestalten möchten. 🚀

 🔹 Rich industrial data

But the key question is:
𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐮𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 – 𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐲, 𝐮𝐧𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐮𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

Last week, I stopped in Brussels, where I had open and constructive exchanges with senior officials at the European Commission – including Michael Hager, Adam Romanovski, Pascal LEARDINI, Mechthild Wörsdörfer, and Bertrand L’Huillier. 

What we talked about:
👉 𝐒𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐲 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐮𝐬 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤. A streamlined digital rulebook – especially through the upcoming #DigitalOmnibus – will help unlock innovation.
👉 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭. Digital technologies, from smart grids to digital product passports or efficient data centers, are key to driving the green transition.
👉 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐭𝐡𝐬. Accelerating the development and deployment of industrial AI will keep Europe competitive in the global AI race.

At Siemens, we’re proud to be an enabler – of the green transition, digital transformation, and the long-term #competitiveness of Europe.

The potential is there. The direction is clear.
But we need to act – now, and #together.

At Siemens, we want AI to be three things: #Robust for industrial grade. Applied with #purpose. Democratized and accessible to #everyone.

As a board member, I always think of AI in three action fields:

🧠 Awareness & Learning – How do we ensure AI reaches everyone across the organization? That includes myself  – we’re all learners on this journey.

⚙️Systemization & Orchestration – Where can AI drive the most value? Some use cases emerge organically, yet we also need structure and orchestration to focus and scale our efforts.

🚀Core Capabilities – Are we moving fast enough to embed AI into the heart of our portfolio? We've done #IndustrialAI since the 1970s, but integrating today’s rapid developments in generative AI and foundational models requires new speed and agility.

I’m pleased to share some of my perspectives on the Siemens Human X AI podcast. Grateful to the hosts, Ulli Waltinger and Arberie  Hakaj, for the thought-provoking discussion.

Let’s continue this important conversation: What are your thoughts on leading with purpose in the age of AI?

Europe has what it takes to lead the next wave of industrial innovation. But to get there, we need to remove what’s holding us back.

For this, we don’t need more complexity, we need #clarity. We need space for #innovation, at pace and at scale. That means accelerating digitalization and scaling back regulation that slows us down. A moratorium on certain laws would help.

I had the opportunity to exchange views on this with Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy at the European Commission. We discussed how major legislation - like the AI Act, Cyber Resilience Act, and Data Act - impacts companies like Siemens. One thing is clear: businesses need clear and meaningful standards, transition periods to adapt and simpler rules to thrive.

We welcome the Commission’s steps to simplify sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements, and to strengthen the Single Market. We’re also looking ahead to the Digital Omnibus package later this year.

At Siemens, we already have the key technologies to help enhance Europe’s global competitiveness - especially in #IndustrialAI. Europe is already a leader in this field. With deep industrial domain expertise and one of the world’s richest sources of industrial data, we are uniquely positioned to turn that heritage into long-term competitive advantage.

Siemens and the #EU share a common vision: building technology that serves people, the planet, and prosperity.

At the AI with Purpose Summit, I had the pleasure of sharing a few impulses with some of the brightest minds in the field of #IndustrialAI.

I spoke about my personal “𝐰𝐡𝐲” - and how it led me to Siemens to lead People & Sustainability - because I deeply believe in what technology can do for people and for society. Our 177-year history is filled with milestones that have connected and empowered humankind - from the first telegraph lines that bridged continents to today’s innovations across industry, infrastructure, mobility, and healthcare.

Here are three thoughts I want to share with all AI enthusiasts:

1️⃣ Purpose doesn’t come from technology alone. It comes from the choices we make in how we apply it. Every company must ask: What gives us the right to play?

2️⃣ We’re at a global inflection point. Technology is advancing faster than human capacity to adapt. We must reflect: Where is the human in the equation? What is the human’s unique value proposition in an AI-driven world?

3️⃣ Companies have a big role to play. Helping people grow - not just through technical skills, but through learning strategies, resilience, and foundational skills like critical thinking - is essential to keeping them relevant throughout their careers.

Let’s never stop asking 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 technology can do for us -
 but start asking more: 𝐰𝐡𝐨𝐦 do we want it to serve, and 𝐰𝐡𝐲?

“With the rise of AI, will I still have a job?”

It’s a question I hear often — and it’s a valid one. But perhaps an even more powerful question is:

“How can I remain employable in a world that’s constantly evolving?” 

Sustainable #employability is about ensuring we have the #resilience, the #adaptability to embrace change positively and to keep our skills relevant over the span of our careers. 

Learning strategies and training „the muscle of learning“ is not only important in response to #AI, but to whatever the future may bring.

Earlier this week in 📍 Singapore, I had the pleasure of sharing the stage with Hao Shuo, CEO of Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and Ishan Palit, Member of the Board of Management and COO of TÜV SÜD, for a conversation on the impact of digitalization on the workforce.

Together, we reflected on the shared responsibility of businesses, governments, and educational institutions in supporting people through this transformation.

Here are a few takeaways:

1️⃣ Humans and AI will work side by side — human interaction is essential to fully unlock the benefits of technology.

2️⃣ Employers must provide individuals with the infrastructure and guidance on what and how to further build relevant skills. People need to be vested in continuous learning. The combination allows the workforce and businesses to transform.

3️⃣ In the face of an aging population and workforce, we should leverage technology to capture and institutionalize knowledge and expertise.

🙌 Transformation takes all of us.

The shape of work is evolving.

Macrotrends such as social, cultural, and demographic changes, and advances in technologies are influencing the labor market. In particular, #AI is having a transformative effect on the way we live, learn, and work. With many regions around the world experiencing an economic downturn and a lack of skilled workers at the same time, how do we ensure that people, businesses, and economies will continue to thrive and be productive in the future?

Visitors to the L.B. Bohle stand at Booth 1619 will see how the company’s latest equipment supports continuous manufacturing and improves pharmaceutical production processes and product development efficiency.

These three technology highlights will demonstrate advances in continuous oral solid dose manufacturing, laboratory tablet coating, and pharmaceutical particle processing.

## QbCon® 1 Truly Continuous Wet Granulation and Drying

The [QbCon® 1 Continuous Wet Granulation and Drying System](https://www.lbbohle.com/pharma-machines-processes/continuous-granulation-and-drying-qbcon-1) represents a significant advancement in continuous oral solid dose production. The system combines continuous raw material dosing, twin-screw wet granulation and drying in one compact, mobile unit.

Advanced features include sophisticated material conveyance, very short residence times in the dryer, automatic exhaust filter self-cleaning and high containment. Integrated control systems increase operational flexibility while enhancing operator safety.

The [QbCon® 1](https://www.lbbohle.com/pharma-machines-processes/continuous-granulation-and-drying-qbcon-1) is designed to deliver narrow residence-time distributions that simplify material traceability in continuous processes. This makes it easier to track materials from raw ingredients to finished tablets, while supporting accelerated scale-up.

Martin Bohle, Dr. és sc.ResearchGate [D-4508-2014](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Martin-Bohle)- International Association for Promoting Geoethics ([IAPG](https://www.geoethics.org/))- [Ronin Research Scholar](https://ronininstitute.org/)@ [edgeryders](https://edgeryders.eu/t/about-us/42); Member of EGU, AGU- recent publication: [Geo-societal Narratives](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-79028-8)- Contextualising Geosciences

Recent research into the societal context of geosciences led modern geo-philosophical frameworks to guide professionals and citizens when interacting with World and Planet Earth. These frameworks combine insights into societal and geoscientific features of the World and Earth into a joint knowledge system ([Bohle et al., 2020](https://issuu.com/wfsf.president/docs/issue_2_2020_hf_final_4_sept/28)). Hence, how they are constructed is paramount.

# Introduction

Geo-philosophical frameworks are epistemic problems at the borderline of different knowledge domains (Renn, 2020). Generally, these frameworks often are tacit about their philosophical foundations, exceptions apart (Frodeman, 2003; Marone and Bohle, 2020). This silence is disadvantageous because the particular philosophical foundation determines how societal practices are understood when shaping the Human-Earth Nexus, the bundle of planet Earth, a planetary technosphere, and a hegemonic culture (Haff, 2014; Lemmens et al., 2017; Rosol et al., 2017; Dyer-Witheford, 2018; Dryzek and Pickering, 2019).

Various modern geo-philosophical frameworks inspect the Human-Earth Nexus; see, for example (Zen, 1993; Peppoloni and Di Capua, 2012; Frodeman, 2014; Cherkashin and Sklyanova, 2016; Nikitina, 2016; Di Capua et al., 2017; Bohle, 2020). These frameworks differ by an epistemic foundation in modern Earth System Literacy from earlier frameworks like noosphere (Vernadsky, 1945; Oldfield and Shaw, 2006; Korobova and Romanov, 2014) or Gaia (Lovelock J., 1979; Lovelock, 1990; Lenton and Van Oijen, 2002; Onori and Visconti, 2012).

The modern geo-philosophical frameworks apply, at least implicitly, realist-materialist epistemologies to understand geoscientific features (Bunge, 2006; Marone et al., 2019). Other epistemological concepts for geo-philosophical frameworks like hermeneutic phenomenology exist (Raab and Frodeman, 2002; Frodeman, 2014). Hence, geo-philosophical frameworks are distinguished by their epistemic foundation and the specific philosophical foundations, which refer to insights into societal features and normative settings.

Martin Bohle, Dr. és sc.ResearchGate [D-4508-2014](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Martin-Bohle)- International Association for Promoting Geoethics ([IAPG](https://www.geoethics.org/))- [Ronin Research Scholar](https://ronininstitute.org/)@ [edgeryders](https://edgeryders.eu/t/about-us/42); Member of EGU, AGU- recent publication: [Geo-societal Narratives](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-79028-8)- Contextualising Geosciences

Recent research into the societal context of geosciences led modern geo-philosophical frameworks to guide professionals and citizens when interacting with World and Planet Earth. These frameworks combine insights into societal and geoscientific features of the World and Earth into a joint knowledge system ([Bohle et al., 2020](https://issuu.com/wfsf.president/docs/issue_2_2020_hf_final_4_sept/28)). Hence, how they are constructed is paramount.

# Introduction

Geo-philosophical frameworks are epistemic problems at the borderline of different knowledge domains (Renn, 2020). Generally, these frameworks often are tacit about their philosophical foundations, exceptions apart (Frodeman, 2003; Marone and Bohle, 2020). This silence is disadvantageous because the particular philosophical foundation determines how societal practices are understood when shaping the Human-Earth Nexus, the bundle of planet Earth, a planetary technosphere, and a hegemonic culture (Haff, 2014; Lemmens et al., 2017; Rosol et al., 2017; Dyer-Witheford, 2018; Dryzek and Pickering, 2019).

Various modern geo-philosophical frameworks inspect the Human-Earth Nexus; see, for example (Zen, 1993; Peppoloni and Di Capua, 2012; Frodeman, 2014; Cherkashin and Sklyanova, 2016; Nikitina, 2016; Di Capua et al., 2017; Bohle, 2020). These frameworks differ by an epistemic foundation in modern Earth System Literacy from earlier frameworks like noosphere (Vernadsky, 1945; Oldfield and Shaw, 2006; Korobova and Romanov, 2014) or Gaia (Lovelock J., 1979; Lovelock, 1990; Lenton and Van Oijen, 2002; Onori and Visconti, 2012).

The modern geo-philosophical frameworks apply, at least implicitly, realist-materialist epistemologies to understand geoscientific features (Bunge, 2006; Marone et al., 2019). Other epistemological concepts for geo-philosophical frameworks like hermeneutic phenomenology exist (Raab and Frodeman, 2002; Frodeman, 2014). Hence, geo-philosophical frameworks are distinguished by their epistemic foundation and the specific philosophical foundations, which refer to insights into societal features and normative settings.

Ich war noch ein Kind, als meine Mutter für drei Wochen durch den Himalaya reiste – und mich bei meinen Großeltern ließ. Ohne Drama, ohne schlechtes Gewissen, ohne Handy. Sondern ganz selbstverständlich mit Mut, einer Portion Gottvertrauen und der Klarheit: Auch eine Mutter hat ein eigenes Leben. Und ich hatte bei Oma und Opa eine großartige Zeit. 😉
 
Heute zum Weltfrauentag denke ich an diese Frau, die mich geprägt hat wie keine zweite: meine Mutter. Als Erste in der Familie machte sie Abitur, studierte, wurde Lehrerin. Sie war alleinerziehend – zu einer Zeit, in der das noch weniger Unterstützung und mehr Vorurteile bedeutete als heute. Und sie hat sich davon nicht definieren lassen. 

Was mich bis heute besonders beeindruckt: Sie hat sich nicht zwischen „Mutter sein“ und „arbeiten“ aufreiben lassen. Sie hat Verantwortung übernommen – für mich, für ihren Beruf als Lehrerin, in der Kirche, für Menschen im Hospiz, für Freunde. Aber sie hat sich eben auch immer wieder für sich selber Raum genommen. Für Dinge, die ihr Freude machen wie Reisen.
 
Am Weltfrauentag geht es aber nicht nur um persönliche Geschichten – sondern auch um Chancengerechtigkeit. Genau hier tragen wir auch als Arbeitgeber Verantwortung und bei der Deutschen Telekom stellen wir uns dieser Verantwortung. 
 
Ich darf an dieser Stelle heute einmal schreiben: Danke, Mama. Für deinen Mut. Für deine Freiheit. Für dein Lachen. Für deine klare Haltung und starken Werte. Für die Wurzeln und die Flügel, die Du mir mit auf den Weg gegeben hast. 
 
PS: und damit sie das auch liest, schicke ich ihr das per email :-).

To me, culture is like gardening.
 
A beautiful garden does not stay the same on its own. If you do not shape it, if you do not nourish or water it, it will stop flourishing. And whenever the weather, the seasons or even the climate is changing, the garden needs special care.
 
The same is true for company culture. We at Deutsche Telekom have a good culture. We have strong values. Our people are proud to be T. They feel they belong. They are engaged. 
But the world around us is changing. Stronger competition. Geopolitical uncertainty. A vibe shift in society.

That is why we decided to evolve our culture at Telekom. And we gave it a new name: T-Style.
 
At today’s Town Hall with Tim Höttges, I explained that gardening is never finished. And we are all gardeners. 
 
As Group, we are defining the frame. We have sharpened our Guiding principles and introduced our three cultural priorities: Performance, Uncorporate, Collaboration. 

However, culture can't be prescribed top-down. As top leaders we can inspire, we have to set the right conditions, we must walk the talk. 
But ultimately, culture is shaped by each and every colleague. By our individual decisions. By the way we work with one another. By the everyday actions we take.

That is why I shared a couple of examples at Telekom. Small, everyday examples that bring T-Style to life:

➡️ Our strong values: More than 100 colleagues donated blood this week here in Bonn – organized by our trainees. A strong example of solidarity and responsibility for the greater good. This is T-Style!
➡️ Collaboration: Our new intranet is being built by a team collaborating across many functions. And more than 10.000 colleagues have already voted for a name. This is what collaboration looks like in practice. Or if my colleagues Rodrigo Diehl and Dr. Ferri Abolhassan drop fire-up messages to me before and during the townhall. This is T-Style!
➡️ The Uncorporate: In my own leadership team, we are testing a simple principle: No decision to make? No meeting. And more time for what really matters. This is T-Style!
➡️ Performance: Whether it is frontline technicians striving for "excellent craftsmanship" for our customers, or colleagues like Ulrich Klenke going the extra mile to make a video truly excellent: this is ambition, devotion and performance in action. This is T-Style!
 
And there were many more great examples today: colleagues and teams who presented projects that truly bring T-Style to life. These projects really deserve the T-Style stamp of excellence! Thank you for sharing your work and your energy.
Thomas Tschersich, Thomas Masicek, Oliver Schmitz, Marcus Mazur, Irena Jakoubkova, Joern Kellermann, Friederike Michaelis
 
A big thank you as well to everyone who joined the Town Hall and to everyone who helped make it happen. 
Michaela Schwinge, Ayse Semiz-Ewald

Ash Wednesday in the Rhineland means one thing: Carnival is over, the costumes are gone – and it’s time for clarity. 

At our oneHR Kick-off, we talked about what we need to deliver in 2026 - and even more about HOW we will deliver it.

We started off with a reflection on the past year. 2025 was not an “easy year” – and still, the HR colleagues at Deutsche Telekom delivered. Big transformations, real progress on skills, our values stayed strong even under pressure, and yes: well-deserved awards across countries and teams. Congrats and thank you to everyone who made that happen!  

Looking ahead, our Culture 2.0 will guide us in 2026 and beyond. 
We call it T-Style. And it consists of: 

➡️Our Group Purpose: We won’t stop until everyone is connected 
➡️Our strong values, our Guiding Principles 
➡️Clear cultural priorities: Performance, the Uncorporate, Collaboration 
➡️And the spirit we want to bring into 2026: optimism.  
 
And our HR priorities we set ourselves for 2026 will be powered by T-Style: 
 
1️⃣  We’ll drive and support transformation: We will keep adapting our organization to what the business needs – responsibly and with our social partners. It’s about doing the hard work thoughtfully, with people in mind.

2️⃣ We want to move from AI usage to impact. Tools are everywhere and more than 75% of our people already use them. But real impact only comes when workflows change. Therefore, we are investing more in our AI enablement, our internal chatbot AskT, as well as in our growth hub platform as a global lever for skills and development.  

3️⃣  We keep our colleagues’ engagement high – and turn insights into measures. Transformation needs energy, pride, and belonging. Therefore, we are introducing a shared engagement metric across all segments. 

4️⃣  We are growing our leaders – more diverse, ready to shape the future. The bar is rising, and we are investing into our talent programs and future skills.

5️⃣  On HR data and IT, we’ll build the foundation and raise the experience for our colleagues. What we’ll work on further: Simplifying heavy processes, improving service quality, clean data and stable systems, and one employee “front door”. 
 
A big thank you to my HR Leadership Team for driving this agenda – and for presenting T-Style today with so much conviction. And THANK YOU to all involved in making this oneHR Kick-off happen!  
 
I said it to my team today, and I’ll keep repeating it:  
Be leading. Be T-Style.

Be leading. Be T-Style.
 
Telekom’s company culture is strong. Our values are well-anchored and our purpose guides us: We won’t stop until everyone is connected.
 
But the world does not stand still. Competition is getting fierce, more and more. We feel a vibe shift: values that once felt widely shared are coming under pressure. And geopolitics is changing the rules of the game. 
 
In this environment, we as Deutsche Telekom are now evolving our culture.
 
We call it: T-Style
 
And today, at our annual Telekom Top Management Team Meeting – #TMTM, I showed what this means for us as leaders. 
 
We are building on the strong foundation of our Guiding Principles. We sharpen them now. To reflect what the moment requires: embracing technology, scaling globally, and the need to be leading. 
 
And we are setting three priorities. They will be our focus areas for 2026 and the years to come:
 
▪️ Performance: Sometimes we shy away from honest, critical conversations about underperformance – and we don’t always recognize high performance strongly enough. It’s clear to us: We have to raise the bar before the market raises it for us.
▪️ The Uncorporate: We complain about bureaucracy a lot when it comes to government agencies. But now it’s on us to act: We’ll challenge our own internal processes, IT systems, and hierarchies. We’ll remove the clutter and make room for ideas and innovation.
▪️ Collaboration: It is often strong within teams already. Now we need even more of it across teams, segments, and countries. Because we win as a network, not as silos.
 
And we already have many examples where we are T-Style today:
▪️ Our teams in networks and services, winning award after award.
▪️ Teams responding in moments that matter – like a power outage in Berlin or supporting communities during floods in Poland.
▪️ The team that brought the Industrial AI Cloud to life, offering data sovereignty in Germany
▪️ Thousands of colleagues giving their time for “Ein Herz für Kinder.”
 
These examples underline what our CEO Tim Höttges said today: culture is not “HR stuff”. Culture is business. It creates value. And it is what differentiates us.
 
From now on, when we as Telekom are at our very best, we will say: “This is T-Style.”
And it’s up to each and every one of us to live this T-Style .
 
That’s why I told my colleagues today, and I will keep saying it across Telekom:
 
Be leading. Be T-Style.
