 🔹 We keep people at the center.
Critical thinking, creativity, and empathy remain uniquely human. AI amplifies these strengths.
 
The future of work will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how we choose to use it.

Two years ago, we took a bold step at Henkel: introducing 8 weeks of fully paid parental leave for all new parents – regardless of gender, family constellation, or location – across all ~70 countries and for all 47,000 colleagues.

We knew it would be complex. But we knew it was the right thing to do – and that it would make us stronger, as a company, as a team.
 
Today, the results from last year speak for themselves. And honestly, they move me.
 
📈 +15% overall uptake vs. 2024
 👨‍👩‍👧 +35% more male colleagues taking parental leave
 
In some countries, this is normal. In others, it’s a radical change. One story from a country in the Middle East region really stayed with me: in 2024, not a single father took parental leave. Last year, 84 male colleagues did.
 
I’m convinced this also pays off for Henkel: attracting talent, enhancing benefits, boosting employee satisfaction and retention – and the numbers prove it. But it’s more than metrics. Teams across Henkel have worked tirelessly to turn this target into action plans and progress. We are: 
➡️ pushing forward the decarbonization of our operations,
➡️ deepening collaboration with suppliers through initiatives like Climate Connect,
➡️ scaling low-emission and circular materials,
➡️ and accelerating innovation in our brands and technologies to reduce footprint along the entire value chain.

These efforts show that our Net-Zero Roadmap is not just a climate target. It’s a transformation of how we source, operate, and innovate as a business. And we are advancing this transformation no matter how challenging and complex it may be.
 
For us, net-zero is not a one-time milestone. It is a responsibility we commit to every single day – for our business, for our partners, and for future generations.

So, one year in, our direction is clear. And our journey toward net-zero continues.

My Daily Question: “Am I a Good Leader?”

Reflection has become one of the most powerful tools in my leadership journey. Every evening on my way home, I ask myself one simple question:
Was I a good leader today?

Not perfect. Just present. 
Did I listen enough? 
Did I create clarity? 
Did I create an environment where others can thrive?
Did I make someone feel valued?

This small ritual keeps me grounded. It reminds me that leadership is a responsibility that shows in the smallest moments. 

Some days, the answer feels like a yes.

You can’t force productivity. You build it through environments where people feel trusted, valued, and empowered.

During my keynote at Mercer’s Human Works Conference themed "All eyes on productivity", I shared how HR is taking the lead as a strategic co-pilot to create environments that help people thrive and, in turn, drive productivity. When designing the employee experience at Beiersdorf, I always return to three beliefs that anchor how we bring our purpose to life.

1️⃣ 𝗔𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀
To truly build an inclusive culture, you need both mindset and action: leaders who understand inclusion and systems that make it real. We reached global gender parity among our leaders in 2023, continue to advance disability inclusion through, for instance, our employee community “Ability” and have embarked on a major journey to upskill all 3,000+ people leaders through our three-month DEI Essentials program with around 70% already finished.

2️⃣ 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳
Enabling everyone to be their best self means giving people the flexibility and security they need to thrive at work and beyond. That’s why we offer flexible working models, including 42 job-sharing tandems (over half in leadership roles), and support our employees in the Moments that Matter through our Global Critical Illness Policy, which provides paid leave, job security, and care for those facing life’s toughest challenges, whether personally or as caregivers.

3️⃣ 𝗪𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝘄𝗲
One of the clearest examples of how care connects people, builds pride, and strengthens engagement across our company is our global Care Beyond Skin Day. Every year, more than 10,000 colleagues across 65 countries dedicate over 60,000 hours to local volunteering projects giving their time, skills, and heart. Our internal research confirms what we feel: 72% of participants say the experience makes them feel more engaged and connected to Beiersdorf

In the end, it’s simple: when people feel seen, valued, and empowered they bring their best selves to work and that’s what drives real productivity. Our role as senior leaders is getting the balance right between raising the bar for performance in an increasingly more difficult environment while strengthening a culture where everyone can thrive. If these two go together, we can unlock productivity.

The closer we stay to our people, the better we lead

Staying in touch with our people is one of the most important parts of my role. That’s why I make it a priority to be approachable and to regularly connect with colleagues across all levels – to listen, to learn, and to exchange perspectives. Our Lunch Connect format in HR is a wonderful opportunity to spend valuable time with colleagues across the organization.

Whether it’s a town hall, a team meeting, or just a chat in the coffee kitchen, every conversation helps me understand what matters most to our colleagues. It’s my daily dose of learning, inspiration, and connection.

Our recent HR Lunch Connect was another great example of how powerful these informal moments can be. We talked about career journeys, our own modernization, the importance of learning and what is next on the agenda.  Every time I walk away with new ideas and a deeper appreciation for the passion and purpose that drive our people.

A big thank you to Talita Queiroz Alves, Gloria S., Anna Nina Börner, and Elisa Maehl for such an open, inspiring conversation and for your honesty, passion, and great ideas! I learned a lot from you!

### Japan’s 2026 plan to promote offshore wind energy in EEZ 

 

By Shunta Doki and Yosuke Nakano of Chuo Oh-Ebashi LPC & Partners 

 

In Japan, the promotion of renewable energy is expected to continue to advance through groundbreaking amendments that allow offshore wind power projects in Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and the strengthening of the Green Transformation (GX) emissions trading system, both of which are set to take effect. 

 

The Act on the Development of Marine Renewable Energy Power Generation Facilities (the amended Act on Promoting the Utilisation of Sea Areas), which enables the installation of marine renewable energy power generation facilities in the EEZ is scheduled to come into force on 1 April 2026. 

 

The Act on the Promotion of Smooth Transition to a Decarbonised, Growth-Oriented Economic Structure (GX Promotion Act) has also been amended, and participation in the Emissions Trading System (GX-ETS) will become mandatory for specified companies starting 1 April 2026.

# 依田 隼弥さんの投稿

「コンテキストエンジニアリング」と、 「ハーネスエンジニアリング」の違いとは？ この2つは似ているようで、 カバーする範囲が全く異なります。 1. コンテキストエンジニアリングとは？ AIに「必要な情報や知識（マニュアル）」を与えること。プロンプトで目標を設定したり、 [xn--AGENTS-oi4el13t5n4bj9f.xn--md-f93a6be5jg2hrc4925lbwla](http://xn--agents-oi4el13t5n4bj9f.xn--md-f93a6be5jg2hrc4925lbwla/?trk=public_post-text)「情報整理」のフェーズ。 2. ハーネスエンジニアリングとは？ コンテキストを内包した上で、AIが失敗しないための「作業環境や自動チェック体制の全体基盤」を設計・構築すること。AIがミスをした際に、二度と同じミスを繰り返さない解決策をシステムとして実装する。 具体的にハーネスエンジニアリングが構築するのは、以下の4つの仕組み。 🔹 ツールの提供とフィードバック AIにテキストを読ませるだけでなく、ブラウザ操作などの権限を与え、実際にテストしてエラーを自己修正させるループを作る。 🔹 アーキテクチャの制約（ガードレール） ルール違反を物理的に防ぐため、カスタムリンターなどを組み込み、エラーを弾くだけでなく「直し方」もAIに教える。 🔹 複数エージェントによる役割分担 1つのAIにすべてを任せず、「プランナー」「ジェネレーター」「評価者（QA）」など役割を分割し、システム全体で連携させる。 🔹 コンテキストの継続的な改善 AIがミスをするたびに、マニュアル（ [AGENTS.xn--md-mb4ad](http://agents.xn--md-mb4ad/?trk=public_post-text)）を自動または半自動で書き換え、フィードバックループを回す。 【結論】 新入社員（AI）にマニュアルを渡すのが「コンテキストエンジニアリング」。 新入社員用の仕事用PCにミスを防ぐソフトを入れ、厳格なチェック体制（評価エージェント）を整備し、確実に仕事が進められるオフィス環境全体を設計するのが「ハーネスエンジニアリング」。 AIを真に自律駆動させるためには、この「ハーネス」の視点が不可欠になる。 [https://lnkd.in/gffFNMqc](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgffFNMqc&urlhash=bIwL&trk=public_post-text)

🌏 Insurance AI: 900+ use cases — and still not scaling 🔍 More use cases do not mean more scale Allianz reports more than 900 AI use cases internally registered worldwide. Yet, speaking at InsurTech Insights, Jason Howes of Allianz UK noted that scaling AI remains difficult, as reported by Insurance Post (Mar 19, 2026). This is not a contradiction. “900 use cases” does not mean 900 scaled deployments. It reflects a portfolio of initiatives — from pilots to partial implementations — across the group. AI is already widespread. But most use cases remain local. They work within specific teams, on specific workflows, under specific assumptions. What they rarely do is scale across: systems workflows decision ownership That is where scaling becomes difficult. ⸻ ⚖️ Not a regulatory issue The EU, under the EU AI Act, pushes for structured, risk-based deployment. The UK, guided by institutions such as the Financial Conduct Authority, takes a more principles-based approach. Different models. Same pattern. Even in more flexible environments, AI does not automatically scale. Because the constraint is not regulatory permission. It is operational integration. ⸻ 🧩 What this means for insurers Scaling AI is not about launching more use cases. It requires: • standardising workflows where decisions can be made • defining clear ownership of AI-driven decisions • designing systems to integrate, not isolate, AI capabilities Without this, AI remains a collection of initiatives rather than an operating capability. ⸻ 🧭 Key message AI does not fail at scale because of individual firms. It fails because large organisations are not designed to absorb it consistently. Hi LinkedIn Community! 👋

I'm excited to share my learnings from the Product Space Assignment on Digital Product Feature Analysis!

🔍 Problem I Explored:
I deep-dived into the UPI Autopay (Mandates) feature in Google Pay, analysing how users experience and manage recurring payments.

💡 Key Learnings:
1. Convenience can reduce awareness:
Autopay simplifies payments, but once set up, users rarely revisit or track their subscriptions, making payments feel “invisible.”

2. The real problem is loss of control, not missing features:
“Users can’t track subscriptions” isn’t the core issue.
👉 The real gap is lack of visibility and control once payments become automatic.

3. Trust in fintech is event-driven:
Users don’t actively think about trust, until an unexpected debit happens.
That moment defines their perception of the product.

🚀 How I’ll Apply This in My Product Management Journey:
💫 Focus more on problem framing vs jumping to solutions
💫 Design for visibility and user control in flows involving automation
💫 Use structured prioritisation (RICE / Impact vs Effort) to guide product decisions

Want to dive deeper? Check out my complete analysis in the attached deck!

The Wisdom of the (LinkedIn) Crowds vs the price of oil?

Here's a quick questions for you - what's the price of oil going to be in 3 months time?

Specifically, the price of WTI in USD/barrel on the 18th of July, 2026 (Give your guess in the comments below, and we'll see how close we get).

I did this exercise with a group of ~100 final year petroleum engineering students at UNSW around 9 years ago. The average from the group was within a few cents of the actual price, nicely demonstrating the premise of the "Wisdom of the Crowds" (https://lnkd.in/gDWU7p-M). 

Because I believe it is often better to quit while you're ahead, I've never run the exercise again. That way I have a 100% success rate (and I can use it as an example of selection bias in my classes). 

But now I'm going to break that rule and run the exercise again. Not because I have a side bet on Kalshi (... but if this works out, lets go!!). But because I'm interested in what the world thinks about the current oil market and where it is heading. So put you best guess below.

To keep it fair for everyone, I'll stop recording entries after a month (17th of May) and post the average a little later (whenever I'm back on linked in). No prizes for whoever gets closest, but I'll let you hold the title of "World Champion" until the next fuel crisis.

Lo scorso sabato abbiamo aperto questa rubrica con una domanda:
chi scrive per un’azienda deve saper scrivere?

Il confronto si è rivelato interessante ed è emerso che, all'interno di questa capacità, si muovono diverse dinamiche.
Chi scrive deve saper contestualizzare quello che produce, rispetto a: mercato, proposta, target, aspettative e bisogni di quel target, nonché alla capacità della proposta di rispondere, in tempi brevi o continuativi, a quelle esigenze e aspettative.

Abbiamo aperto un orizzonte all’interno del quale adesso cominciamo a muoverci.
La domanda che vi propongo oggi è questa:

Cosa significa saper scrivere per il business?

Non mi riferisco ai tre segreti per scrivere bene, perché sinceramente lasciano il tempo che trovano.

Ma a cosa significa, nella vostra esperienza, raccontarvi qui su LinkedIn, o raccontare l’azienda di cui fate parte...

Vi riporto una storia vera per rompere il ghiaccio.
In questi giorni ho avuto un confronto con un imprenditore.

Persona molto capace, concreta e attenta alla gestione delle risorse economiche.
Ha deciso di iniziare a utilizzare Claude per gestire la sua comunicazione, da solo.
Non ha una particolare dimestichezza con la lingua, si occupa di altro.
Ma ha scelto di sostituire una funzione interna, quella della comunicazione, affidandola completamente alla macchina, che gestisce lui.

Ha iniziato a lavorarci, ha studiato diversi materiali formativi che si trovano anche gratuitamente in giro su questa piattaforma.
E alla mia domanda: “come ti trovi?”, ha risposto:

“Claude è fantastica. Riesco a scrivere benissimo, molto meglio di prima. Performa da D*o!”.

Poi ho letto i contenuti... 

A parte che l'Altissimo non è pervenuto,
nemmeno del resto: non c’è alcuna gestione della brand voice!

A monte mancano indicazioni che permettono allo strumento di lavorare in quella direzione.
E soprattutto manca il passaggio più profondo:
la capacità di sapere quali aspetti debbano essere osservati e costruiti prima della produzione del testo.

Gli scritti sono pieni di epanortosi enfatica, di triadi gratuite e di quel “davvero” che è diventato il nuovo "cruciale" negli output generativi.

Qual è il punto?
Pensare che una macchina possa scrivere per il proprio business, senza una competenza linguistica a monte, senza un lavoro di analisi e di gestione fondato, espone a un rischio concreto:

quello che scriviamo ci fa tuffare nel mare della mediocrità, che oggi vediamo ovunque nella scrittura, in particolare su questa piattaforma.

Dov’è l’analisi del contesto?
Dov’è l’analisi del pubblico?
Dov’è l’analisi della relazione che si vuole costruire?

🚀 Basics of Human Resource (HR) Department – A Quick Overview

Human Resources (HR) is one of the most important departments in any organization. It plays a key role in building strong teams, maintaining workplace culture, and ensuring smooth employee management.

✅ Core Fundamentals of HR Department:

🔹 Recruitment & Hiring
HR identifies the right talent for the organization by sourcing candidates, conducting interviews, and managing the hiring process.

🔹 Employee Onboarding
After hiring, HR ensures the employee joins smoothly by handling documentation, orientation, and training coordination.

🔹 Employee Engagement & Relations
HR works on maintaining a healthy work environment, handling employee concerns, and ensuring proper communication between employees and management.

🔹 Performance Management
HR supports appraisal processes, goal setting, and employee development programs to improve productivity.

🔹 Policy & Compliance Management
HR ensures company rules, labor laws, and organizational policies are followed properly.

💼 Recruiter Role in HR

A Recruiter is the backbone of the hiring process. Their key responsibilities include:

📌 Understanding job requirements
📌 Sourcing candidates through job portals, LinkedIn, referrals
📌 Screening resumes & shortlisting profiles
📌 Conducting initial HR rounds
📌 Coordinating interviews with managers
📌 Negotiating salary and offering letters
📌 Maintaining ATS and recruitment records

A recruiter’s goal is to bring the best talent into the organization.

💰 Payroll Management – A Key HR Function

Payroll management ensures employees are paid correctly and on time. It includes:

✅ Salary calculations
✅ Attendance & leave tracking
✅ PF, ESI, tax deductions
✅ Payslip generation
✅ Incentives, bonuses, and overtime calculations
✅ Compliance with government regulations

Payroll is important because it builds employee trust and ensures financial accuracy.

🤔 Are you making these 3 deadly mistakes with your LinkedIn posts?

Here’s how to fix them:
1️⃣ Mistake: Writing for Everyone ✨ When you try to appeal to everyone, you connect with no one. 
Fix: Write for your ideal audience. Address their specific pain points and goals. Example: “Struggling to optimize your LinkedIn profile? Here’s a quick guide to get started.”
2️⃣ Mistake: Skipping the Hook ✨ If your first line doesn’t grab attention, your post won’t get read. Fix: Start with a bold question, surprising fact, or relatable statement. Example: “Did you know 80% of LinkedIn posts fail because they’re too generic?”

3️⃣ Mistake: No Call-to-Action ✨ If you’re not guiding your audience, you’re missing engagement opportunities. Fix: End every post with a clear CTA. Ask a question, invite feedback, or spark a conversation. Example: “What’s your go-to strategy for LinkedIn engagement? Let’s discuss!”

💡 Pro Tip: Successful LinkedIn posts are specific, engaging, and actionable. Avoid these mistakes, and watch your engagement soar.

Introducing Hyperagents: an AI system that not only improves at solving tasks, but also improves how it improves itself. The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) demonstrated that open-ended self-improvement is possible by iteratively generating and evaluating improved agents, yet it relies on a key assumption: that improvements in task performance (e.g., coding ability) translate into improvements in the self-improvement process itself. This alignment holds in coding, where both evaluation and modification are expressed in the same domain, but breaks down more generally. As a result, prior systems remain constrained by fixed, handcrafted meta-level procedures that do not themselves evolve. We introduce Hyperagents – self-referential agents that can modify both their task-solving behavior and the process that generates future improvements. This enables what we call metacognitive self-modification: learning not just to perform better, but to improve at improving. We instantiate this framework as DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H), an extension of the DGM in which both task-solving behavior and the self-improvement procedure are editable and subject to evolution. Across diverse domains (coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math solution grading), hyperagents enable continuous performance improvements over time and outperform baselines without self-improvement or open-ended exploration, as well as prior self-improving systems (including DGM). DGM-H also improves the process by which new agents are generated (e.g. persistent memory, performance tracking), and these meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across runs. Yesterday, I had the honor of moderating an incredibly inspiring World Economic Forum session on AI and the future of work, with two visionary leaders Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach. Yesterday’s discussion made it clear that while AI continues to transform our world, it is our people – with their creativity, adaptability, and judgment – who are powering the future. 

We came away with three clear lessons leaders can use when empowering people to lead with AI:

1. Optimism over anxiety. The conversation is shifting, and employees are increasingly hopeful about what AI can do for them and their organizations. Success starts with leaders who champion and empower their teams to see challenges as opportunities. 

2. AI is for everyone. Universal adoption is key. AI should amplify every employee’s impact, regardless of their role. Commit to championing AI literacy in your organization, ensuring every person has the confidence and skills to thrive alongside AI tools. 

3. AI is the tool, but people are the power. Your people are the engine of transformation – fuel them. As leaders, we must invest in both cutting-edge tools and world-class training equally. When we do both, we do more than adopt AI – we lead the future.

Thank you to Judson and Carl for sharing your perspectives in such an insightful discussion. I look forward to helping shape the future of work we discussed – a future where AI amplifies and empowers what makes us uniquely human. #WEF26 Workday Microsoft

Cancer has affected my life in very personal ways—my dad fought prostate cancer for more than 17 years and my mom faced stage 3b breast cancer. And just last year, one of my routine screenings came back with an irregular result. Like so many people who face this type of unexpected news during their preventive screenings, my first reaction was fear. Thanks to Merck’s comprehensive benefits, I was able to quickly get follow-up testing and a biopsy — and fortunately, everything came back clear.

These tough moments remind me of how much access and support matter. That’s why I am so proud of the progress our company has made in support of cancer prevention and early detection. In under a year, we have expanded access to WHO-recommended screenings (breast, cervical, colorectal), HPV-related cancer vaccinations, and the time and flexibility to use these services—now reaching more than 96% of employees and their families across 71 countries. The team continues the hard work to extend these benefits where they are not yet available.  

I’m so grateful to everyone at Merck who made this possible and to all those working tirelessly to advance cancer prevention, early detection and care.

AI is already more powerful than what most organizations are able to realize today.

This idea kept coming up at Lake Como last week in conversations with business leaders. The challenge is turning that potential into new ways of working, new skills, and real business impact. That was the focus of the SAP Italy Executive Summit, where more than 100 leaders came together to discuss how to build future-ready organizations in an AI-driven world.

In my conversations with Lavinia Spingardi, Carla Masperi, and Augusta Spinelli, we explored why so many companies still struggle to unlock AI at scale: Many are still trying to layer AI onto fragmented data landscapes, siloed processes, and legacy operating models. As a result, AI remains isolated in use cases instead of transforming how work actually gets done.

Organizations that move ahead take a different approach: they redesign workflows end-to-end, integrate AI directly into core processes, and clearly state where decisions are augmented by AI, and where accountability remains human.

During an interview with Giulia Cimpanelli for La Repubblica, another dynamic became very clear: many organizations are currently in the productivity dip of AI transformation. That dip exists because work is being rebuilt while results are not yet visible. People are learning new skills, roles are shifting, and processes are being redesigned at the same time. The critical mistake is to interpret this phase as failure. In reality, it’s where the real work happens – rebuilding skills, processes, and ways of working.
This is exactly the moment where leadership matters most. Being clear about direction, transparent about what’s changing, and giving people the space to learn and adapt, even when things feel less efficient at first.

Grateful for the conversations, the openness, and the shared ambition to not just adopt AI, but to truly turn it into value for business and people.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Thank you to Ricarda Engelmeier, Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. Horst Wildemann and everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful discussion.

The vision is simple yet bold: connecting young African talent with German companies to learn, grow, and ultimately win as one. 

17 years on, that vision feels more relevant than ever. Actively engaging with the cohort – listening to their journeys, exchanging ideas, and learning from their hopes, challenges, and achievements has moved me deeply. It reaffirmed that cross-cultural collaboration isn’t just good for business; it’s essential for a peaceful future. 

As President Steinmeier put it: “Wir Deutsche wollen unsere Beziehungen zu afrikanischen Ländern nicht nur festigen und stabil halten, wir wollen sie ausbauen. ... Gerade jetzt, in dieser Zeit der Umbrüche, Kriege und Konflikte, gerade jetzt setzen wir Deutsche auf Weltoffenheit – auf Vernetzung statt auf Abschottung, auf Freihandel statt auf Protektionismus, auf mehr statt weniger Zusammenarbeit!”  

His call for openness, connectivity, and deeper collaboration is a clear compass for business – and it mirrors SAP’s commitment to partnership, innovation, and shared growth. 

To all participants of AFRIKA KOMMT! 13: thank you for your ideas, energy, and determination. Keep your networks alive, keep challenging assumptions, and keep paying it forward. 

We are proud to have been part of AFRIKA KOMMT! from day one, and we look forward to welcoming future cohorts to SAP to keep building bridges. The bridges we build today will become the paths others walk tomorrow – let’s keep building, together.

Die Bitkom #TRANSFORM26 in Berlin war für mich ein wertvoller Impulsgeber: Wenn es um Transformation geht, müssen Politik und Wirtschaft eng zusammenrücken.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.


Bundesministerium für Bildung, Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend | DIW Berlin - German Institute for Economic Research

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

Europe has what it takes to lead the next wave of industrial innovation. But to get there, we need to remove what’s holding us back.

For this, we don’t need more complexity, we need #clarity. We need space for #innovation, at pace and at scale. That means accelerating digitalization and scaling back regulation that slows us down. A moratorium on certain laws would help.

I had the opportunity to exchange views on this with Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy at the European Commission. We discussed how major legislation - like the AI Act, Cyber Resilience Act, and Data Act - impacts companies like Siemens. Sustainable #employability is about ensuring we have the #resilience, the #adaptability to embrace change positively and to keep our skills relevant over the span of our careers. 

Learning strategies and training „the muscle of learning“ is not only important in response to #AI, but to whatever the future may bring.

Earlier this week in 📍 Singapore, I had the pleasure of sharing the stage with Hao Shuo, CEO of Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) and Ishan Palit, Member of the Board of Management and COO of TÜV SÜD, for a conversation on the impact of digitalization on the workforce.

Together, we reflected on the shared responsibility of businesses, governments, and educational institutions in supporting people through this transformation.

Here are a few takeaways:

1️⃣ Humans and AI will work side by side — human interaction is essential to fully unlock the benefits of technology.

2️⃣ Employers must provide individuals with the infrastructure and guidance on what and how to further build relevant skills. People need to be vested in continuous learning. The combination allows the workforce and businesses to transform.

3️⃣ In the face of an aging population and workforce, we should leverage technology to capture and institutionalize knowledge and expertise.

🙌 Transformation takes all of us.

Industrial history and personal history are rarely far apart. That connection became very real when 91-year-old Paul Diestelhorst opened his photo albums and gave us a glimpse into a life shaped by the power station in Frimmersdorf. A rare and valuable insight.
 
The demolition of cooling tower Q at the end of February made the connection very tangible. The enormous steel and concrete chimney was built in the 1960s as part of what would become Europe's largest power station at that time. It is a significant part of our company's history and of the region's industrial identity.
 
At the age of 19, Paul came to Frimmersdorf in search of work. What followed was an entire working life with RWE – from power plant operator to control room operator to foreman. He knew every corner of tower Q. And at this advanced age, he witnessed the demolition of the very structure that he helped build and operate for decades.
 
Stories like Paul’s demonstrate to me what makes RWE stand out as an employer: the recognition of every single employee’s contribution. Day in, day out, shift after shift, on land and at sea.
 
With RWE’s accelerated phase-out of coal by 2030, a chapter of industrial history is coming to an end. And at the same time, our story continues. The Frimmersdorf site, for example, will be transformed into an innovative digital and transformation hub, and key parts of the power station will be preserved in the spirit of industrial heritage conservation. That is what RWE stands for: knowing and respecting our history yet always looking ahead and shaping the future.
 
Thank you, Paul, for everything you have achieved and given to #TeamRWE.

Cybersecurity is a top priority for RWE. After all, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure are no longer the exception – they are part of our everyday reality.

Yesterday, I spoke about precisely this topic at the Digitalk meets ZACTALK event (Digitale Stadt Düsseldorf e.V.) at XPONENTIAL Europe and highlighted three key perspectives:

▪︎ Cybersecurity is a key factor in building trust: for our employees, for our partners and for society, which relies on a reliable energy supply at all times.
▪︎ Cybersecurity as a strategic issue: cybersecurity is managed just like any other key management and risk issue: transparently, taking a risk-aware approach and an integrated view of resilience.
▪︎ The corporate culture dimension: sustainable cybersecurity is effective not only in systems, but also in day-to-day actions and through mindset. It requires informed, attentive, and empowered employees and managers who actively exemplify security. At RWE, we bring this to life through a variety of formats – from web-based trainings and phishing simulations to live hacking sessions and escape rooms.

AI is a particular focus. It is fundamentally changing the risk landscape, including in the field of cybercrime. Precisely because AI-powered cyberattacks specifically target the human factor, human judgement becomes more important – not less so.

For RWE, this means that cybersecurity does not end with prevention. Strong detection and response capabilities, clear responsibilities and a security culture that is put into practice form the foundation for a secure energy transition without disruption.

It is not every day that industry, law enforcement and the military sit down together to discuss security and economic policy perspectives. Thank you for this enriching discussion Manfred Boudreaux-Dehmer, Markus Hartmann, Jens Elstermeier and Stephan Schneider for chairing.

Warum will niemand mehr Führungskraft werden?

Das wollte DER SPIEGEL von Heike Bruch wissen. Sie ist die Herausgeberin der St. Galler Jugendstudie, die drei Kipppunkte ausgemacht hat, wieso junge Menschen keine Lust mehr auf Führungspositionen haben.

Vorgesetzte wirken oft ausgebrannt und in einer Arbeitsmühle, die wenig erfüllend wirkt. Junge Menschen nehmen Strukturen als alt und starr wahr. Und: Führungskräfte spüren oft eine Überforderung oder das Gefühl, am Limit zu arbeiten, sodass sie ihre Führungsaufgaben am liebsten wieder abgeben möchten.

Die Quintessenz – und auch mein Erleben aus meinem beruflichen Alltag: Es fehlt dem Nachwuchs nicht an Ehrgeiz, sondern mitunter an Möglichkeiten, Verantwortung zu erproben, und auch an Vorbildern, die zeigen: So sieht gute Führung aus. So macht Führung Spaß.

Wir bei RWE sind uns unserer Verantwortung, Führungskräfte kontinuierlich auszubilden, bewusst. Zunächst einmal ist es sicherlich erfreulich, dass wir bei RWE keinen Mangel an Mitarbeitenden haben, die Führungsaufgaben übernehmen möchten. Nun liegt es an uns, eine Umgebung zu schaffen, die sich von der oben skizzierten deutlich unterscheidet. Dazu zählt, dass wir unsere Führungskräfte und Potenzialträger auf ihrer Reise begleiten und unterstützen.

Für den Gesamtkonzern haben wir unser Führungskräfteprogramm, unsere RWE Executive Journey, weiter geschärft. In Linie mit unserem Purpose, unseren Unternehmenswerten und unseren erfolgskritischen Verhaltensweisen haben wir ein gemeinsames Führungsverständnis definiert: Unsere RWE Leadership Principles. Diese Führungsprinzipien folgen klaren Standards und formulieren eine klare Erwartung, wie gute Führung bei RWE gelebt wird:

▪︎ Lead for Business Impact
▪︎ Lead to Deliver
▪︎ Lead for Team Success

Eine Umgebung zu schaffen, in der unsere Mitarbeitenden am besten wachsen und wirken können, liegt an uns. Wir begleiten unsere Führungskräfte auf jedem Schritt ihrer Reise und bereiten sie strukturiert auf ihre Rolle vor. Das gilt für das gesamte Spektrum von der ersten Führungsrolle, der Weiterentwicklung als Führungskraft oder einem Neueinstieg bis zum Gesellschaftswechsel.

Wichtig ist uns auch: Leadership ist nicht immer eine lineare Entwicklung, sondern hochindividuell: Es gibt auch Möglichkeiten zurück in Fachpositionen, geteilte Führungsrollen oder Sabbaticals als Möglichkeiten, neue Perspektiven kennenzulernen.

Unsere RWE Executive Journey unterstützt kontinuierlich, leitet an und ermutigt, den Schritt in die Führungsverantwortung zu gehen. Ein großer Dank an die vielen HR Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem gesamten Konzern, die gemeinsam RWEs Weg an dieser Stelle unterstützen.

Ich bin schon sehr gespannt, wie sich die Ergebnisse in unserem Unternehmen widerspiegeln werden. Denn ich bin überzeugt: Führung ist attraktiv!

Bleiben wir Anwender oder ist unser Anspruch bei KI ein anderer?
 
Unter anderem darum ging es bei „Allianz der Chancen trifft… Lars Klingbeil“ gestern in Berlin. Die Arbeitswelt geht in die nächste Phase über. Und die gelingt nur im Zusammenspiel zwischen echter und künstlicher Intelligenz. 
 
Im Fokus der Gespräche stand daher, wie eng Finanzpolitik, technologische Entwicklung und Beschäftigung miteinander verbunden sind. Investitionen in Infrastruktur – wie zuletzt in die KI-Fabrik in München – sind zweifelsohne eine wichtige Grundlage. Entscheidend ist jedoch, ob wir Anwender bleiben oder den Anspruch entwickeln, Weltmarktführer für KI-gestützte Geschäftsmodelle zu werden – und ob wir KI dabei konsequent menschenzentriert denken. 
 
Dafür braucht es die Mitarbeitenden aller Unternehmen, die sich in der Allianz der Chancen zusammengeschlossen haben. KI und Mensch müssen dabei Hand in Hand gehen. Auch in dem Bewusstsein, die richtige Tonalität zu treffen, um auf die Ängste vieler Menschen zu reagieren. Mein Eindruck ist, dass wir uns bei Unsicherheit oftmals wieder an alten Verhaltensmustern bedienen, die wir eigentlich schon geglaubt, überwunden zu haben. Hier wünsche ich mir ein gemeinsames Narrativ, eine gemeinsame Strategie aus Politik und Wirtschaft.

The way AI is shaped will shape the world!
 
The question therefore is: Do we want to remove biases or reinforce blind spots? One alarm signal for the latter is that various studies indicate only around 22-30% of global AI talent is female.
 
At RWE, however, we strive to do the former. We want AI in our organisation to reflect the perspectives, creativity, and empathy of everyone – not just a few. This week I had the pleasure of joining the launch event for our Women in AI network. The network brings together women from different functions across teams and countries, creating a space to connect, learn, and experiment. It’s about more than representation – it’s about enabling women to actively and responsibly shape AI in ethical, inclusive ways.
 
During the discussion I shared my view of AI as a key enabler of digital transformation and the energy transition. And about what is needed in terms of a strong foundation for AI to scale. It's what I call a golden triangle consisting of:
▪️HR – to bring purpose and heart
▪️IT – to drive innovation
▪️Security – to provide the trust that allows us to move fast without breaking things
 
Together, they form the foundation of an organisation where AI can act as a co-pilot, supporting employees and freeing up time for creative, strategic work by humans. This is where women make a real difference. Women often bring strong domain expertise, ethical awareness, and empathy. Diverse teams reduce blind spots and help build robust AI solutions that are fairer and more sustainable. 
 
This was a successful start to the network, and I am already very excited to see the first tangible results. Thanks to Thomas Denny and Marina Sverdel for the lively discussion on stage and huge congratulations to Gülnaz Öneş and the women on the AI core team for making this network possible.

“Turning points”
“Geopolitical storms”
Uncertainty is no longer the exception, it’s now part of leadership.
 
How do uncertainty and a rapidly changing world shape the way we lead? This was a topic in the panel discussion with Colette Rückert-Hennen we had at  The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) German Symposium.
 
From my personal perspective – being responsible for HR, IT and Security – the challenge is even more fundamental: We are moving from an era of efficiency to an era of agency. The past decades, leadership was about managing “Human Resources”. Now, AI is finally taking the 'robot' out of the job. It is absorbing the management chores, the data-drudgery, and the administrative friction. This creates spaces. New possibilities. 

The big question for us on this panel is: What would be the wisest way to fill the newly created spaces? Our shared conviction: If we manage to fill it with Human Agency - transparency, radical vulnerability, and shared leadership - we turn uncertainty into our greatest competitive advantage. My goal is to use technology as a multiplier, not a replacer, so that our collective time becomes our company’s most valuable asset.

Are women better prepared for uncertain times, as there is something called the "female" leadership style? 

I try to avoid stereotypes, but research shows that in times of high stress, there is the temptation to revert to autocratic styles when the world feels 'Brittle' or 'Incomprehensible' (BANI). It feels safe to have one person 'set the course.' But I have to argue the opposite. Autocracy is a bottleneck. In an era where AI agents are processing data and making micro-decisions in milliseconds, an autocratic leader becomes the slowest part of the system. An autocratic leader who pretends to have all the answers creates a fragile organisation. A leader who shows vulnerability and transparency creates a resilient one. In a BANI world, collaboration is a survival skill, not a 'soft' skill. And so is Diversity!

Thanks to Hartmann Ilka for your moderation, and again to Colette Rückert-Hennen. It’s always a pleasure to share perspectives and the stage with you.
 
Actually, this thoroughly inspiring day began already in the morning with a meeting at the German Embassy in London where we had the opportunity to speak with the British Ambassador, H.E. Andrew Mitchell, and the German Ambassador, H.E. Susanne Baumann. This exchange provided valuable international perspectives on leadership as well. A day fully packed with great discussions.

My first business trip this year, and I'm returning with a lot of insights and impressions.

The last days in Vietnam were dense and fully packed. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City: Two site visits with our partner FPT Software, where parts of our IT services are delivered and where we are currently further exploring our Best Shoring Model. Every conversation focused on capability, reliability, and long-term performance rather than short-term optimisation. 

The same mindset was apparent at FPT University. A very holistic view on education: Computer science is central, of course, but every student is required to also study English, practises Vietnamese martial arts, and learns to play a traditional musical instrument. Performance, they showed me, grows not from technical skills alone, but from discipline, balance, and cultural grounding. That combination is remarkable. 

This perspective carried into a panel on Women in Tech and Energy, which I opened with a speech while wearing a beautiful traditional Vietnamese dress. We spoke about technology, but the deeper question was how to prepare people for what comes next. At RWE, a human-first approach means using AI to support people: to simplify work, increase efficiency, and create space for strategic thinking, creativity, and developing new capabilities.

I see women playing a dedicated role in the AI transformation. We must lean in when AI models and LLMs are trained, ensuring that the future AI world is at least as diverse as today's. And this commitment comes to life in the field, as we noticed during our visits to Offshore Delivery Centres and the AI Campus in Saigon, where we saw AI already processing vast data sets in real time and accelerating development cycles from months to days, all underpinned by a performance culture built on clarity, ownership, and ambition. 

I leave Vietnam with gratitude for the openness and generosity of everyone who shared their insights – especially Chu Thi Thanh Ha and all colleagues at FPT Software. 

Happy Lunar New Year next month to everyone celebrating.

Let's start the year with a view!
 
After taking you on a virtual tour of a wind turbine, today we're heading to the “heart” of the offshore wind farm: the substation.
 
What you see here is the offshore substation of our Kaskasi wind farm, 35 km off the coast of Heligoland. The substation is the central hub where electricity from all turbines comes together before heading to shore. From the outside, it might seem like just another platform at sea, but inside it’s a giant tangle of components and connections, all designed to make the flow of electricity reliable and continuous.
 
What kind of work goes into this heart of an offshore wind farm? Nothing less than an engineering masterpiece in manufacturing, heavy-lift vessels to transport the thousands of tonnes of topside components, and absolute precision during the “marriage” at sea – the installation of the topside onto the foundation. 
 
Once completed, the wind turbines turn, the generators produce electricity, and this is fed into the relevant grid connections via the substation. Sounds simple – but take a look for yourself! It’s easy to forget, from the outside, just how much care and coordination goes into making everything work. 
 
Looking ahead, RWE Offshore Wind will deliver four construction projects with a total capacity of 4.8 GW and continue providing clean, reliable electricity from our wind farms. Considering the dedication that goes into every detail, it’s clear that none of this would be possible without #TeamRWE.

The areas of application are diverse, ranging for example from process improvements to site layouts for offshore wind farms or weather models for our trading business.

It brings users and technology together, in a kind of laboratory environment where employees can bring specific concerns and then experiment with them. Leadership is changing. And it makes me genuinely proud to see how these shifts are taking shape within RWE.
 
Last week I met Melanie Peter and Claudia Neumann, two colleagues who share one role as Head of Corporate Finance EU & APAC. What they have created goes far beyond dividing tasks. It shows what shared responsibility can mean when it becomes a real form of leadership.
 
The idea of job sharing grew over time – from a conversation about flexibility and new ways of leading. Both worked part-time, both were ambitious, and both realised how well their strengths complemented each other. What began as a simple thought became a shared leadership model they shaped with intention.
 
Job sharing gives two leaders the space to combine responsibility with balance. It allows them to bring different perspectives to one role and gives their teams continuity and clarity. For us as an organisation, it helps people stay on a leadership path during different phases of their lives and strengthens how we work together overall. 
 
When I spoke with Melanie and Claudia, I was struck by how clearly they structure their work. They have defined who leads on which topics, they keep each other informed on the issues that matter most and they step in for one another without hesitation. Strategic decisions and key people topics are made together, which gives their teams consistency and a clear direction. Their partnership is focused, confident and deeply human, and it shows how shared leadership can be both decisive and balanced.
 
Now, after a year in their shared role, their conclusion is clear: it works. It delivers. And it keeps evolving. This is not an experiment. It is progress in motion.
 
For me, their story captures what leadership at #TeamRWE is about: trust, curiosity, and the courage to rethink what is possible together. Because transformation is not a strategy on paper. It starts with people who lead differently – and it ends with a company that grows stronger because of it.

Ready for new perspectives? Step inside an offshore wind turbine — at least virtually 😉.
 
Offshore wind is one of our key technologies in generating low-carbon electricity. Close to 200 metres above sea level is where ambition meets teamwork. #TeamRWE currently has around 5 GW of installed capacity of offshore wind under construction — in parallel, across three countries! Earlier this week, we celebrated milestones that three out of four construction projects finalised foundation installation and are ready (or already in full swing) for turbine installation.
 
Reason enough to share with you a glimpse of what it looks like in one of our powerful 9-MW turbines at our offshore wind farm Kaskasi, which is located 35km off the coast of Heligoland: 81-metre blades, a rotor span roughly the size of three football fields. Pure engineering brilliance. But take a look for yourself and enjoy the insights from boat landing up to the nacelle!
 
And while new turbines keep rising, our Operations and Maintenance teams make sure everything runs smoothly across a growing number of wind farms and turbines. Their work keeps this progress alive — steady, reliable, and safe. I am grateful for everyone who makes that possible every single day.

We are transforming our core business. Major investments, new technologies, innovative ideas – these are obvious and visible. But our technological transformation to a low-carbon business model is only one dimension. 
 
A recent study by Fraunhofer HNFIZ demonstrates the complexity of transformation. It explored what factors enable companies to manage transformation successfully. Using AI, the researchers analysed more than 250,000 scientific publications and identified 31 key factors grouped into five dimensions: 
 
• Leadership and governance 
• Culture and collaboration 
• Resources and intellectual property 
• Technology and data 
• Ecosystems and markets 
 
The message is clear: technology is only one part of the picture. Human connection, learning and trust turn transformation into lasting progress. 
 
At RWE, this is our daily reality. The energy transition reaches every corner of the company — technical, organisational and cultural. Every day, #TeamRWE is adapting - taking on new responsibilities, sharing knowledge in new ways, and finding practical ways to support one another through constant change. 
 
As leaders, it is our responsibility to create the right environment for this to happen, spaces for learning, opportunities for open dialogue and building the confidence that everyone can help shape this journey. Because transformation doesn’t happen to people; a joint commitment turns change into lasting success.

Turning safety into something you can experience – that’s the idea behind our new Safety Tour at the RWE Campus in Essen.
 
Health and safety is our number one priority at our power plant sites and in our offices. We have created an interactive guided tour with seven stations across the campus. Topics include ergonomics, occupational health care, emergency management, fire extinguishers and first aid, escape routes and assembly points, business travel, and walking safely on campus. Each stop turns theory into practice with clear information and practical tasks. This hands-on format brings theory to life and fosters active dialogue in an engaging manner, as managers and employees work their way through the tour together.
 
I really like our new safety tour because it’s a smart way making health and safety tangible and part of our everyday work - not just a checklist!
 
Many thanks to Kay Paßlack, Heike Bruckmann and Frank Topp for developing and implementing this inspiring format.

Social engagement is something that is particularly close to my heart. In addition to my private commitments, I also have the chance to do this professionally in my role as Deputy Chair of the Advisory Board of the RWE Foundation. Today, I would like to introduce you to one of our projects that shows the impact we can have on young people's lives by ensuring that every child and adolescent has a fair start in life, regardless of their circumstances.
 
Centrepoint’s Upstream England project focuses on prevention through social participation to stop youth homelessness before it begins. Building on the successful Geelong Project model from Australia, it is the first early intervention programme of its kind in England. The project was established with support and guidance from Llamau, which has led similar pioneering early intervention work in Wales.
 
Together with schools in London and Manchester, the project identifies children at risk of future homelessness due to poverty, family stress, or difficult childhood experiences. Using an annual digital survey, it recognises early signs of vulnerability and offers personalised support, including conflict resolution strategies, training in nonviolent resistance and access to mental health and addiction prevention services.
 
This early, community-based approach helps ensure that young people stay connected, supported, and hopeful, preventing homelessness before it becomes a crisis. The project has been running successfully since March 2023, with RWE Foundation funding supporting delivery from July 2025 to June 2028. With its initial capital of €125 million, the RWE Foundation is able to support projects that give young people fair chances, help communities and make a difference where it matters most. 

We cannot solve the world’s problems alone, but together we can have a real impact.

Mental health has arrived in our daily lives: in everyday conversations, in break rooms, and even in board rooms. That’s exactly where it belongs. As the world becomes faster and more unpredictable, mental health challenges are rising and so is the need for awareness, empathy, and real support.
 
For me, looking after my mental wellbeing starts with knowing what gives me energy and what takes it. For almost 20 years, rituals like hiking and fasting have helped me switch off, reset and recharge my mental batteries. Every summer I go on a pilgrimage along the Camino de Santiago and it’s my way to pause, recharge, and practice my own ‘letting go’. Taking time to relax (without guilt!) really makes a difference for me. 
 
Even in business, mental health challenges are rising. That’s why open conversations and real support matter. At RWE, we try to make it easy to speak up and get help when you need it, through support programs or practical tools. Sometimes it’s the small steps that matter most.
 
Being open, asking for support and taking time for ourselves. These small steps can make a real difference for our mental wellbeing. Let’s keep normalising these conversations and supporting each other at work and in everyday life.

Between the past and the future lies a passion for energy and stories that connect generations. Some call it tradition, others continuity. For me, it’s the chance to introduce you to the Klevers family, who’ve been part of RWE for five generations.
 
We had a great conversation about their family’s long-standing connection to RWE, going all the way back to Lars’s great-great-grandfather. Lothar has been with RWE since 1981 and has seen a lot of changes over the years. Now Lars Klevers is continuing the tradition as part of #TeamRWE. I really enjoyed our exchange and hearing their views on how the company and the energy sector are evolving, especially in the Rhenish lignite area.
 
Meeting Lars and Lothar was something special. Their passion and positive outlook for the future really left an impression on me. Their perspective got me thinking about how tradition and change can go hand in hand.
 
Thank you, Lars and Lothar, for sharing your story with me. It was great to hear about your journey and what being part of #TeamRWE means to you.

Wie sollen wir richtig mit KI umgehen? Wahrscheinlich eine der entscheidendsten Fragen unserer Zeit. Eins ist klar - die Antworten müssen aus mehreren Perspektiven betrachtet werden. Was könnte dafür besser sein als ein zeitloser Begleiter: das gute alte Buch!
 
In meinem Kapitel des Buches „Quality Economy – Limitationen quantitativer Ökonomie, Potenziale qualitativer Ökonomie“ beleuchte ich unter anderem, wie Mensch und KI Hand in Hand arbeiten können, um in ganz unterschiedlichen Arbeitsbereichen echte Synergien zu schaffen. Bei RWE nutzen wir KI beispielsweise um HR-Prozesse effizienter zu gestalten. Auch in technisch-operativen Geschäftsbereichen setzen wir KI bei der Überwachung und Instandhaltung von Solar- und Windparks ein. Mit unserer KI-Governance stellen wir sicher, dass künstliche Intelligenz stets transparent bleibt, den Menschen in den Mittelpunkt rückt und unsere Unternehmenswerte widerspiegelt.
 
Darüber hinaus widmet sich das bei Springer erschienene Buch zentralen Themen wie der digitalen Transformation, dem Klimaschutz, sozialer Gerechtigkeit und einem bewussten Umgang mit Ressourcen. Es zeigt konkrete Ansätze, wie ein nachhaltiger Wandel von Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft aussehen könnte. Herausgegeben von Prof. Bernd Thomsen, Simone Thomsen, Florian Schreitter Ritter von Schwarzenfeld und Dr. Oliver Everling vereint es 27 Beiträge von Expertinnen und Experten aus den Bereichen Wirtschaft, Technologie und Gesellschaft.
 
Ein spannendes Buch mit interessanten Ansätzen und Perspektiven zur Gestaltung der Wirtschaft von morgen!

Energiewende live erleben? Das gibt’s bei uns im Rheinischen Revier!
 
Bei meinem Besuch dort konnte ich sehen, wie echte Transformation aussieht. Gemeinsam mit Kemo Razanica, Matthias Dürbaum und Thomas Körber und dem #TeamRWE stand der Tag ganz im Zeichen von Austausch, Teamwork und beeindruckenden Einblicken.
 
Ein Highlight war der Besuch eines unserer Solarparks, der das Ergebnis der starken Zusammenarbeit zwischen RWE Power und RWE Onshore Photovoltaik Europe & Australia ist. Hier zeigt sich, was Teamgeist und echte Kooperation ausmachen – alle packen mit an, teilen ihr Wissen und bringen die Projekte gemeinsam voran.
 
Besonders spannend war der Austausch mit den jungen Kolleginnen und Kollegen. Frischen Ideen, neugierige Fragen und neue Perspektiven haben mich nachhaltig beeindruckt. Dieser Spirit ist es, der den Wandel möglich macht und deutlich zeigt, wie die Zukunft gestaltet wird!
 
Ein weiteres allgegenwärtiges Thema: die Sicherheit vor Ort! Es ist sehr eindrucksvoll zu sehen, wie konsequent Maßnahmen umgesetzt werden – nicht nur zum Schutz aller Mitarbeitenden, sondern auch präventiv, damit Gefahren erst gar nicht entstehen.
 
Vielen Dank an das gesamte #TeamRWE für einen Tag voller spannender Einblicke in die tägliche Arbeit! Glück auf!

The first half of 2025 was marked by steady progress and continued momentum!
 
RWE delivered good financial results throughout the first half of the year, but numbers alone don’t tell the full story. Behind every project is the teamwork, expertise, and dedication that truly drive progress in delivering energy solutions.
 
Thank you, #TeamRWE, for making this progress possible every single day. Let’s keep moving forward together to achieve our goals and shape the energy transition!

Können wir KI als Werkzeug einsetzen, um die Energiewende nachhaltig und verantwortungsvoll zu gestalten? Und wie hilft sie uns, die Arbeitswelt von morgen zu gestalten – bei stetigem Fokus auf den Menschen?
 
Transformation ist mehr als nur technologische Innovation. Bei RWE steht eines im Mittelpunkt: Transformation gelingt nur gemeinsam. KI soll so eingesetzt werden, dass sie echten Mehrwert schafft, durch Entlastung der Teams, indem sie zum Beispiel repetitive Aufgaben übernimmt und Arbeitsprozesse effizienter gestaltet. Während wir neue Strukturen schaffen, begleiten wir unsere Mitarbeitenden aktiv durch den Wandel. Wir berücksichtigen die verschiedenen Lebensphasen und Bedürfnisse unserer Belegschaft. Flexible Arbeitsmodelle, individuelle Entwicklungsperspektiven und technologischer Fortschritt greifen bei uns ineinander, um allen Mitarbeitenden Wege zu eröffnen und sie in der Energiewende mitzunehmen.
 
Genau darüber habe ich mit Alex Hofmann im Podcast von Table.Media gesprochen. Vielen Dank für den anregenden Austausch!
 
Ein Podcast über die Möglichkeiten und Entwicklungen der Energiewende und den verantwortungsvollen Einsatz von Technologie.

Visiting our sites always demonstrates the significance of the work of #TeamRWE, and my recent trip to the Clauscentrale power plant in Maasbracht, Netherlands, was a great example of this. As one of the largest gas-fired power plants in the region, Clauscentrale plays an important role in the Dutch energy system. Today, it supplies electricity to almost two million households, highlighting its contribution to providing reliable power for homes and businesses.
 
As part of RWE Generation’s portfolio, Clauscentrale provides the flexibility needed to maintain grid stability and support a secure energy system. Side Fact: Finding smarter, more flexible solutions to meet the demands of a changing energy landscape is the approach behind RWE Generation's portfolio consisting of Gas, Hydropower, Hydrogen and Battery Storage Systems.
 
During my visit, I met Jens Fuhrmann, the power plant manager and head of the Gas Cluster NL, overseeing operations across multiple sites. Jens and the whole team shared a detailed overview of the power plant’s history, design, and daily operations. Clauscentrale has truly experienced the challenging environment of the energy industry in the tension field between security of supply and economic efficiency. And it’s great to see that the LTI remains at zero!
 
Thanks to the entire team at Clauscentrale for their hospitality and the valuable insights they shared. Visits like this highlight the level of expertise, collaboration, and perseverance required to ensure a reliable energy supply for millions of people. Behind every megawatt produced, there are skilled professionals working with precision and care!

In business, quarterly results and annual reports guide decisions. But what is success if it doesn’t last? Focusing only on short-term gains risks losing sight of the bigger picture and the long-term value that is essential for the future.

Today’s leaders face a balancing act: growth versus cost discipline, innovation versus stability, and talent investment versus efficiency. These competing priorities challenge us to focus on creating growth and driving meaningful transformation.

At RWE, change is a constant. We build adaptable systems, regularly reviewing and evolving them. This fosters a culture of reflection, collaboration, and improvement, where innovation and continuous improvement guide our work and decisions.

Technology drives progress at RWE, but its true value lies in people. Skills like empathy, creativity, and logical thinking are irreplaceable, enabling us to harness technology as a tool for meaningful progress and long-term value. Of course, HR plays a key role! By combining AI and automation with strategic investments in lifelong learning and leadership development, we empower leaders to amplify their impact, enable others to succeed, and spread innovation and resilience.

How do we measure true value? We challenge the view of people and technology as cost factors. Instead, we see them as essential, long-term investments driving growth and future success.

Being future-ready means asking the tough questions and having the courage to act on the answers. That’s where true transformation begins.

More than 10 gigawatts in operation and nearly 4 gigawatts under construction show that the U.S. is one of RWE’s most important markets. The demand for electricity from solar, wind and battery energy storage remains strong, even as we see some shifts in the external environment.

During my recent trip to the U.S., I visited our teams in Valhalla and Chicago. Joined by our US CFO Ingmar Ritzenhofen in the 2 townhall meetings on site, we could exchange with the teams on a wide range of topics. This experience was a strong reminder of how valuable in-person exchange still is.

In Chicago, I visited our new office for the first time, which brings together teams from renewable development and trading in a modern space full of energy. Our commercial experts play a key role in securing long-term energy supply agreements with partners like Meta, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft. These partnerships are essential for success in a competitive market.

During my visit, I also appreciated the opportunity to connect in smaller settings, such as the Women’s Breakfast and Women’s Lunch. These moments created space for open conversation and valuable exchange among female colleagues.

One clear takeaway: it is not just about the size of our pipeline, but about how we deliver projects when conditions change. In a dynamic market like the U.S., staying competitive means staying flexible, making smart decisions and relying on strong local teams. That’s what makes the difference and why this market will continue to be a key pillar of our global renewables business.

Seit 25 Jahren hat die RWE AG einen eigenen Betriebsrat – ein guter Anlass, um innezuhalten und zurückzublicken. Ein Vierteljahrhundert vertrauensvolle Zusammenarbeit zwischen Arbeitgeber- und Arbeitnehmerseite, geprägt von Offenheit, Respekt und dem gemeinsamen Willen, gute Lösungen zu finden. Im besten Sinne einer funktionierenden Sozialpartnerschaft. 

Der Konzern hat sich in den 125 Jahren seiner Unternehmensgeschichte stark verändert. Strategien wurden neu gedacht, Strukturen angepasst, Aufgaben neu verteilt. Der Betriebsrat ist über viele Jahre personell konstant geblieben und hat diesen Wandel engagiert begleitet. Besonders schätze ich, dass wir auch in kontroversen Diskussionen im Dialog bleiben – konstruktiv, lösungsorientiert und mit Blick nach vorn. Viele wichtige Themen wurden angestoßen: die Förderung von Frauen und Eltern, Jobsharing-Modelle oder die Kita Lumiland sind nur einige Beispiele.

Dieses Jubiläum ist vor allem eine Gelegenheit, Danke zu sagen. An alle ehemaligen und heutigen Betriebsratsmitglieder: Für euren Einsatz, eure Haltung und euren Beitrag zur Entwicklung von RWE. Ein besonderer Dank geht an Sandra Bossemeyer. Du warst von Anfang an dabei und führst den Betriebsrat bis heute mit Klarheit und Herzblut. Deine mutige Entscheidung, diesen Weg zu gehen, hat viel bewegt. Auf viele weitere Jahre guter Zusammenarbeit!

The current energy market is shaped by both growth and uncertainty. Demand continues to rise, driven by electrification, AI and digital infrastructure. At the same time, we are facing inflation, higher interest rates, supply chain constraints and geopolitical tension. The political direction of the energy transition is still under discussion.

At RWE, we tackle this complexity with focus, discipline, and collaboration to move forward. Therefore, we brought together our top 60 global HR leaders for our recent HR All Hands Offsite, synchronising our HR strategy to the current and upcoming challenges — with a clear focus on Leadership Development and AI. The insights to RWE’s broader strategic goals from my colleague Michael G. Müller made our path even clearer.

My key takeaways from the inspiring session with Prof. Dr. Yasmin Weiß: the speed of change will keep increasing, the AI era is just beginning, and our human USP will make the difference. Excellent corporate and leadership culture as well as organisational agility will make the difference.

My focus remains on two key areas: driving our IT transformation and further developing our leadership architecture. Both essential for enabling change. Once again, this gathering showed what #TeamRWE can achieve when we work together, stay open and move in the same direction.
